speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: DUTCH ONIONS
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO IMPOSITION OF DUMPING DUTY ON IMPORTATIONS
speechtext: Will the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) state whether, in view of the very grave threat to the onion growers of Canada arising from the fact that the Canadian market is being flooded with a huge surplus of Dutch sets of onions that are being offered at as low a figure as one and a half cents per pound, and in view of the further fact that if any relief is to be afforded there must be immediate action by the government, the government has yet decided to impose the dumping duty, as was done in the spring of 1931?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue):
maintopic: DUTCH ONIONS
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO IMPOSITION OF DUMPING DUTY ON IMPORTATIONS
speechtext:
The responsibility is not that of the governor in council but of the Minister of National Revenue, and the matter has been fully considered. It was discovered upon investigation that seventy-five per cent of the stocks of onion sets now in Canada are not in the hands of farmers or growers of onion sets but in the hands of dealers; and, as the effect of a dumping duty would be to benefit the dealers rather than the growers, and as the persons who would be injured would be farmers who are purchasing onion sets, it is not deemed advisable to impose a fixed valuation for duty purposes.

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, March 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Dunning for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Blackmore.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I do not know whether this is the third or the fourth time on which I have had a few observations to make upon this motion. Apparently the time available at any one sitting was not very long.
In view of the observations made the other day by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) I should now like to direct attention to the problem of international payments and their effect upon our general monetary position. It will be recalled, perhaps, that in this country during the last few years we have had a good deal of difficulty with respect to exchange, and we have had discussions on more than one occasion with respect to favourable and unfavourable balances.
International balances consist, of course, of visible and invisible items. We refer to the visible items generally as commodity balances, and we now include in commodity balances gold, it being no longer part of our standard but merely a commodity. On the other hand the interest we pay abroad, the freights we pay, the insurance premiums, royalties on moving pictures, dividends, and all matters of the kind constitute the invisible outflow of money from this country.
In 1926 we had reached the point in the development of our trade where a substantial favourable balance was indicated. We had 275-6 millions in our favour at the end of the year, and we had an additional 31-5 millions with respect to gold. We had also an item which we cannot consider too carefully, namely the tourist trade, which consists of the amount of money left by tourists in this country; and had it not been for that item during the last ten years our position on more than one occasion would have been one of extreme difficulty. In 1926 the tourist trade amounted to 102-5 millions. The total of all these accounts during the year 1926 amounted to 409-6 millions. Against that we had an adverse balance with respect to freight, shipping, also insurance, royalties and dividends and matters of that kind, and we had to make net interest and dividend payments amounting to 201 millions. So that after we deducted that from our favourable balances we had left a
favourable international balance of 189-1 millions, which we are told would be represented by the movement of that much capital out of this country for investment elsewhere.
In 1927 our commodity balance-that is, the goods we export and import-had fallen to 138-9 millions. Our gold had risen to 25-5 millions and tourist expenditures left in Canada amounted to 129-8 millions, a total of 294-2 millions. That year our interest and dividend payments amounted to. almost as much as the previous year, but our favourable balance amounted only to 63-2 millions. Now that in itself, I submit in view of what is happening in the country at the moment, indicates a condition to which any government should pay the closest attention having regard to the circumstance that England has recently been directing attention to a similar significant fact in her own economy. In 1928 our trade on commodities was favourable to the extent of 131 millions. Gold had risen to 89-2 millions, and the tourist expenditure stood at the very substantial sum of 167-7 millions making a total in our favour of 387-9 millions. But again, there were payments in respect of freights on shipping insurance and the like, and in addition, dividends and interest, and these stood at the very large sum of 221 millions, so that our favourable balance was 131-7 millions, nearly twice that of the preceding year.
In 1929, and I can recall the circumstance very vividly, as many hon. members no doubt will, during the discussions in parliament it seemed to some of us at least that the danger signals were waving. There are differing views in this regard; if there were not there would be no political parties. At any rate we believed that these matters were of serious moment, and we find that our commodity account showed an adverse balance of 131-3 millions; that is to say, our imports exceeded our exports that year-commodity exports-by 131-3 millions. And it will perhaps be within the memory of some hon. members from western Canada that that was the year the Winnipeg Free Press so strenuously advocated the farmers holding their wheat and not being misled by Argentine sales and prices. Further, also, it will no doubt be recalled that in the succeeding speech from the throne it was pointed out that we had in hand practically the last year's crop.
Now that is important because it contributed, of course, to the adverse commodity balance. Then, before taking care of all these matters, we had the following points to con-

sider. First, we had a gold balance, favourable, of 74'5 millions; our tourist expenditures had risen to the very large sum of 187-8 millions; but we had to pay that year, as well as freight insurance and the like, interest and dividends, 260 millions odd; so that on all our accounts we had 195-8 millions of an adverse balance.
That is an important fact and one which I think cannot readily be overlooked in view of existing conditions; indeed, if it were not for that fact I perhaps would not feel that I was warranted in taking up the time of the house at the moment to direct attention to the matter.
Then we come to the year 1930. It might be said that our friends opposite were in power during the whole of that year, from the point of view of the figures, although they went out of office during the last half of the year. That year we had a total adverse commodity balance of 122-1 millions. Gold had fallen 2-7 millions and the tourist expenditure-I direct attention to this very significant factor -was still at the high figure of 178-8 millions. The payments that we had to make outside of this country rose to 288-6 millions and on balance we had an adverse showing of 286-5 millions.
Remember that long before the stock boom had collapsed international security vras no longer what it once had been, and investors throughout the world became apprehensive of all their foreign holdings. That, therefore, is some explanation of the condition that then arose. Bear in mind also that in 1930, at the end of the year, this country had an international adverse balance of 286-5 millions. I said, and I believe my hon. friends opposite wall agree, that that was a significant fact with respect to the depression that was upon us. But the danger signals had been flying in 1929. They continued to fly in 1930 and matters became so acute in that year that there developed the situation to which I have directed attention, wherein there was an adverse balance of 286-5 millions. Confronted with that situation, what did w-e face? Such a situation, unless it is arrested, means national bankruptcy; there can be no gainsaying that, and no one attempts to deny it. I suppose that most hon. members of this house realize the discussions that took place in England in that connection. She was having a continued adverse trade balance notwithstanding the vast interest payments that were coming to her from investments abroad; and that is why economists there were agreed on the question of raising tariffs.

We come now to the year 1931. Things were very bad but we had reduced our commodity trade balance to the small figure of 17-4 millions. Our gold item had gone up to 90-1 millions and our tourist expenditure still stood at the large figure of 174-4 millions. I point out that this tourist item has been the one thing that has been of such value to us during all these years in relation to our international trade balance. As I say, it amounted in that year to 174-4 millions and the gold item was only 90 millions. So that one gets some idea of what the tourist trade has meant to this country. After taking the gold and the tourist trade and allowing therefor, we find that we had to provide for payments abroad the large sum of 279-8 millions, and after the balance was taken between the two, visible and invisible, we found that we had reduced our balance, still adverse, to 78-3 millions, an improvement of over 200 millions over the previous year.
I am not going to discuss here at length the reasons why that was brought about, but it was brought about by the imposition of dumping duties for one thing, and, of course, the tariff that we passed as an emergency measure in the fall of that year. I point out these two factors because they are of tremendous importance in view of the international situation at the present moment. I also point out that in the fall of 1931 Great Britain went off the gold standard. England had gone on the gold standard in 1925 or 1926, too soon after the war, some people thought. In the fall of 1931 the gold in the Bank of England was exhausted and she went off the gold standard and passed a statute indemnifying the Bank of England for what had been done during the Friday and Saturday when they should not have carried on their operations owing to the depleted state of their gold.
Now we come to 1932. In that year we had a favourable commodity balance of 73-7 millions. We had gold that year of 73-1 millions, and our tourist income, although it was dropping, still retained its vigour to the extent of 155 millions. In other words, it was more than twice the value of the gold which we had available to correct our adverse position. Again we find that we had been able, by the financial action taken, to reduce somewhat the extent of the payments we had to make abroad. That year interest and dividends were against us to the extent of 261-8 millions. So that when the balance was finally struck we found that we had reduced the adverse balance to the triflng sum of 22-3 millions.

In that year the empire trade agreements were initiated and came into effect. We entered on the year 1933 with much more confidence than we had had in the preceding year. In that year our favourable commodity balance stood at 146-6 millions; gold had risen to 87-8 millions. The tourist income had dropped to 66-2 millions. Altogether these items made up 300 millions in our favour. Then we turn to the external payments for interest, freight, royalties, etc.; that year, by the operations carried on, interest and dividends were 224-3 millions. We then found ourselves not only out of the red but with a credit balance that amounted to 20 millions. That represented the culmination of efforts that commenced in 1930 and had been carried on-the Minister of Finance says not with much vigour, but our opponents of those days used to say with too much vigour- with all the vigour at our command at any rate, utilizing the machinery of tariffs and dumping duties and everything we could command by legislation and otherwise for the purpose of restoring our position in the international world.
In 1934 we increased our commodity balance, that is of exports over imports, to 148-1 millions. Gold now had risen to 109-6 millions. Tourist income was a little better than the year before, at 82-4 millions, making a total with respect to these items of 340-1 millions. By the operation of our reduction of interest rates, and of course, I am sorry to say, by the diminution of dividends that our enterprises were paying abroad, representing investments of nearly $7,000,000,000 of United States capital in this country, we found that our payments abroad had been reduced to 211-6 millions. So that we finished the year with a favourable balance on visible and invisible items of 74-8 millions. That was the year in which you might say we definitely began to show an upward movement in the curve of return to prosperity. The lowest level was in 1933, then it began slowly to go up, as pointed out by the banks in their returns.
In 1935 we had a total favourable commodity balance amounting to 192-7 millions; gold had risen to 116-7 millions, with tourist income once more improving, so that in that year we had 123-2 millions from tourist expenditures, making a grand total of those three items of 432-6 millions. Here again we find interest and dividend requirements lessening; in that year they amounted to only 208-6 millions. In 1935 therefore we had a favourable visible and invisible balance on international account of 180-9 millions.
Compare that with the situation that was left us as a legacy in 1930. If the student of affairs is concerned to look for analogies, look at the condition of this country to-day. What is the position? The figures show that last month our exports to the United States fell from 36 to 17 as compared with the preceding month. That is a significant fact, and it marks exactly what took place in 1929 and 1930. To-day our exports are diminishing, our imports increasing. We met the situation with our dumping duties and emergency tariff, and I suggest that with these danger signals flying it is the duty of the government to take some cognizance of the situation and prepare us against that day which is fast upon us. In making that observation I am merely recording views which find expression not here only, but in every part of the world. Everyone in the world realizes what these dangers and difficulties are.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman does not suggest that we had prosperity when he had these high trade barriers, between 1930 and 1935, does he?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I suggest just what I said a moment ago, that by reason of the action which was taken, prosperity had begun in this country in the latter part of 1933; it continued upward in 1934, 1935 and 1936, and in 1937 it stopped sharply. I suggest that prosperity did not come in a single day or a single year. Depression did not come in a single day or a single year. I again point out to the minister that, cognizant of these conditions, realizing that these adverse balances were rolling up against us, we adopted the only methods to which we had recourse to meet them, and accomplished the purpose we had in mind. And more; we not only accomplished it, but we obtained from the manufacturers of this country their undertaking that they would not raise their prices except in respect of increased costs of raw materials. They kept their word, with but one single exception of which I know, and the consumer did not pay. To add the tariff to the cost of goods for the purpose of showing the incidents of the tariff between these years is entirely beside the question and wholly wrong.
Let us look at 1936. A new government came into office; and the Minister of Finance talks about the vigour with which it acted. Show me what was done in 1936 that was not merely maintaining what was done between 1930 and 1935. Did your excise tax remain at three per cent? Is it there yet? Did your tariff duties remain where they were before, except with respect to United States

items? And with regard to the United States tariffs remember it was a Republican tariff, the highest tariff the United States ever had. It was not a Democratic tariff. Instead of reducing their tariff by legislation they provided that the president should have power to make treaty agreements, for what purpose? For the purpose of extending favoured nation treatment, to all the nations of the world if you will, but the amount of reduction could be only fifty per cent and no more. Fifty per cent of that ad valorem tariff was fifty per cent of an average of almost forty-five per cent; fifty per cent of the whole, adding the ad valorem to the specific, meant fifty per cent of sixty per cent, the highest tariff in the world. That was what it meant; that is what it means. And more; under that agreement he could not make a free item dutiable or a dutiable item free. Congress would not authorize him to do so, and congress placed a limitation on the period over which these agreements were to extend. That is why we have quotas. That is why I objected in this house, and our friends objected. That is why we will continue to object to an agreement that imposes a quota upon the exportation to a market of 125,000.000 from a market of 11,000,000, when they have free entry for all their products in the market of 11.000,000. Those are the reasons,why we at least tried to make the position clear.
Then in 1936, with the government continuing the very policies against which they had railed, what was the trading balance? Look at the result of it, from the day we endeavoured to correct the position by the emergency tariff of 1930, with the undertakings to which I have referred. Let us look at it. We find that in 1936 the commodity trade balance had increased to 322-2 million dollars. That was not brought about by any action that was taken within twelve months, after the change of government. That was the maintenance of that principle upon which we had accomplished these results. That is known by all. We had gold increasing to $131,000,000; we had tourist expenditures once more increasing up to $156,000,000, making a total under those three items of 609-2 million dollars. Interest and dividend payments, freight payments and payments abroad amounted to 233-8 million dollars, because by this time some of our dividends had been increased, and the money pouring out of this country to service this seven billion dollars of investments here had increased, so there we had 233-8 million dollars. And we had a net total favourable balance of 323-6 million dollars, brought about by the maintenance of those provisions which had

been made for the purpose of correcting what had commenced in 1929.
Perhaps it is not pertinent at this moment to enter into a discussion with regard to the export of capital from this country, and various other matters to which reference might be made. Sufficient for my purpose it is to say that the statistical department has furnished us with an indication that our trading balance at the end of December, 1937, was still favourable, but was falling as compared with the preceding year. Our commodity trade was favourable to the extent of $212,000,000. Gold had risen to $145,000,000. The tourist trade had increased to $170,000,000, and interest and other payments abroad amounted to $247,000,000. Other items totalled $63,000,000, still leaving us a credit balance of $217,000,000 at the end of the year. But look at what has happened since. It has been only three months, but they have been three months which, it seems to me, more nearly make the analogy between 1929 and 1930 very important to any government, and to the government of this country in particular. There you have the flags flying distress signals. They are apparent. There is no business man who has not seen them. Go and look in the factories. Go and look at the reduction in the number of workmen in the factories. Go and look at the business man's attitude towards the problems with which he has to deal. You find the signs everywhere. What are we doing about it? AVe have the significant railroad situation. Do you realize that during one of these three months our nationally owned railway did not earn its operating expenses? Is that not something to think about?
With these other signs to which I have directed attention, with respect to these matters, I shall close that phase of it, but I have in my hand a document issued by the United States government concerning trade between Canada and the United States. It is their version of their relations to us, not our version of our relations to them. I fancy most hon. members have received copies of this document. I commend to my fellow members of this house a consideration of these words:
Canada is our largest single foreign market for finished manufactured products.

I shall not do more than commend this document to the consideration of hon. members opposite, because it contains month by month the statement of imports into the United States from Canada of various kinds of commodities. And it will be noted that in 1937 our exports, which are their imports, fell to $24,876,000. It might be of interest to note that even in those sad, dark days of 1935, in May of that year the exports from this country to the United States were over $27,000,000. The returns which came the other day from the office of the Minister of National Revenue indicate that in the month of February they fell to $17,000,000. Those were our exports to- the United States. But you do not notice a very great diminution in imports, do you, from there?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Is it right to assume from my right hon. friend's remarks that at the present time the tariff against the United States should be increased?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I did not say anything about the United States. But I do say this, that if this country's integrity is to be maintained it may become necessary to take those steps of an emergency character which were taken in 1930 to safeguard the life of Canada.
What is more, I could-but I do not propose to do so-deal with questions having to do with the trade of this country, under the empire agreements. That matter may properly remain for another occasion. I have dealt with this primarily for the purpose not of discussing trade but of dealing with the monetary side of it. The stabilization of exchange must always be one of the foremost considerations in the mind of any one responsible for the exchequer.
When England went off the gold standard -it is idle for me to say to the house what

hon. members know as well as or better than I do; I apologize for even making the observation at all to the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean)-the immediate effect was to have our dollar sensitive to the falling of sterling exchange. Our dollar in the United States financial mind is so closely connected with the pound sterling that we can maintain our dollar at par when you have the British pound at par or thereabouts. The pound is now about five dollars, and our dollar remains at par.
The question arose at one time whether as soon as England went off the gold standard we should not resort to some kind of inflation. It will be recalled that fluctuations of the pound were very marked-so marked, in fact, that the pound in New York did fall to 83.30, a very low quotation indeed. I suppose it must be within the minds of most hon. members that steps were taken here to endeavour to prevent our being made bankrupt, because we had so -many obligations to meet in the United States. At this point may I quote briefly from a statement I made before the board of trade at Toronto at the beginning of 1933:
Another difficulty, of considerable importance to us all, was the depreciation of currencies. When the pound sterling fell from 84.8(5 to $3.70 ($3.30 in New York) and the currencies of all other European countries and of Japan fell to the level now obtaining, it created additional difficulties for the Canadian people. I will not stop to speak of the methods by which we endeavoured to grapple with these difficulties, except that I would like to say a word with respect to the question that arises out of the depreciated currencies. Sometimes I find suggestions from those who have given little study to the problem to the effect that all that is necessary for us to do in Canada is to embark upon a policy of inflation. What does inflation mean? Nine out of ten that I ask have no answer, except they say, you will have two dollars where you had only one before.
Gentlemen, may I point this out to you; geographically, we are part of the North American continent. Who by taking thought can add a cubit to his stature? Who by taking thought can change Canada from being a part of North America to being a part of Europe?
The Prime Minister made an observation somewhat like that the other day.
Gentlemen, I invite you to remember that fundamental fact, that the Dominion of Canada geographically is part of the North American continent. And it gives me no joy to remind you also that financially it is in the same position. But frank recognition of a fact is absolutely essential if you are going to deal with the problem that it raises. In this year of grace, the Dominion of Canada must meet in the United States of America, Canada and Great Britain, for principal and interest on Dominion loans, direct and guaranteed, provincial loans, direct and guaranteed, loans of municipalities and a few public corporations,

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
the enormous sum of $684,149,048. Of this $323,346,120 represents principal and $360,802,928 represents interest. You will note the interest alone is almost a million dollars per day, including Sundays and holidays. We have to provide this by renewals of our promissory notes or by payment. And of this vast sum there is due in the United States of America $266,124,100. Of this sum $109,392,776 represents principal due this year, and $156,731,324 interest. The obligations of the dominion due in the United States this year for principal and interest direct and guaranteed aggregate $108,244,576. Similar obligations of the provinces amount to $70,600,073; of the municipalities to $25,136,536 and of public corporations to $62,142,915.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, it becomes apparent even to the most thoughtless of us all that we had a situation to meet which required that we should do everything possible to stabilize the exchange situation, in other words, to give value to our dollar; and one of the reasons why balances, visible and invisible, become important, is that if we have a favourable trade balance with the United States it means that we at least have some dollars there with which to meet our obligations.
I want to refer to another statement I regard as somewhat important because it was made at the imperial economic conference held in Ottawa in 1932. The situation we were there dealing with was world trade, not exchange. These are the words used by me at the imperial economic conference of 1932, as reported at page 116:
One of the most important effects of the fall in prices is the increased burden of the fixed charges payable on our governmental and private obligations held abroad, chiefly in the United States and the United Kingdom. Canada is an important debtor country; on January 1, 1932, total British and foreign investments m Canada were estimated at 6-4 billion dollars, against which is an offsetting Canadian investment abroad of 1-8 billion dollars.
It is a little less than that now.
A careful compilation of the amounts we will have to pay abroad during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1933, indicates a total of $362,000,000, or over a million dollars a day (exclusive of Sundays). Of this total, $233,000,000 represents interest and $129,000,000 represents maturing principal. Moreover, declining commodity prices have greatly increased the drain of this interest and amortization bill upon our national production. As one dollar to-day will purchase at wholesale 48 per cent more than it did in 1929, the real burden of the service charges on these foreign obligations has increased from $362,000,000 to $535,750,000.
It is true that there would be some offset because of the fact that these commitments include interest and principal payable to Canadian nationals who will exercise the privilege of cashing their coupons and bonds in NeV York when the terms of the security allow that alternative. Such payments will eventually come back to Canada. It is estimated that possibly from 25 to 50 million dollars will
return to this dominion. (There is a wide range to this estimate because it is impossible to estimate with precision.) This leaves a net balance of service charges payable abroad amounting to from $310,000,000 to $340,000,000 which in terms of the 1929 dollar would be equivalent to from $460,000,000 to $500,000,000. The total value of our wheat and wheat flour exports in the record year 1929 was $494,000,000; in the fiscal year ended last March it had fallen to $135,000,000.
From another angle these obligations abroad are of major significance in the consideration of Canada's monetary policies. Most of them; are payable in New York or optionally in Canada and New York, or Canada, London and New York. Where such options exist the premium on New York funds makes it practically inevitable that payment should be demanded in New York funds. This means that during the year ended next March a maximum of over $279,000,000 will be payable in the United States. England's going off the gold standard was followed by a drastic decline in the price of our dollar on the New York market.
I should like to ask my friends opposite, especially the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), to listen to this;
The effect which this action by England had on Canada is difficult to exaggerate. It has resulted in a struggle to maintain the national integrity.
Hon. members have perhaps heard me say that too often.
It was necessary for us to increase customs duties not for the purpose of protection, but to maintain the balance of our national position. We had either to face bankruptcy or restrict imports. At one time, our dollar fell as low as 75 cents in the New York market. To-day the premium on New York funds is only 14 or 15 per cent, but even with this premium the increased burden to the individual corporation or government of servicing these foreign loans is obviously a heavy one. ii ^ >
e<iually clear that the depreciation of the Canadian dollar and the fluctuations in New York exchange increase the difficulty of refunding old loans and floating new issues in the American market. This is particularly important in view of the fact that since the war the United States has been our chief source of capital imports. Of the 6-4 billions of foreign investments in Canada referred to above, over 3-9 billions or nearly 62 per cent are owned m the United States, and only 2-2 billions or 34 per cent, in the United Kingdom.
The figures are somewhat changed now as shown by the bureau of statistics, but I shall not take time to correct them.
From 1924 to 1931, the United States absorbed over 41 per cent of the public issues of Canadian bonds, whereas the United Kingdom's purchases averaged less than 2 per cent of the total as compared with approximately 75 per cent before the war. At the end of 1931 Canadian banks had 83 million dollars loaned on call in New York and over 100 million dollars in bank balances in that market. Under present conditions, therefore, the relationship of our dollar to the American dollar is bound to be of great significance to Canada.

Finally, the evils of fluctuating exchanges are especially injurious to Canada because of the importance of foreign trade in our national life. With only ten million people Canada ranks fifth among the nations in imports and sixth in exports, whereas on a per capita basis we rise to third place in exports and to third or fourth in total foreign trade (depending on the year selected). Normally, about 20 per cent of our productive activities, it is estimated, are directly involved in commodity exports. Nor, as was pointed out in other discussions this morning, is the major portion of this foreign trade with empire countries. In 1930, for instance, 46 per cent of our exports of Canadian produce went to the United States and 67-9 per cent of our total imports came from that country. With the whole British Empire, on the other hand, the proportions were onlv 33 per cent for exports and 20*3 per cent for imports. For Canada, therefore, stable exchanges with gold standard United States^ as well as with the empire countries are a vital necessity.
Mark you, the United States was then, on a gold standard basis.
With our southern neighbours, also, tourist expenditures and other forms of commercial and social intercourse bulk large. Invisibles play an important part in our international balance of payments. Tourist expenditures m this country, for instance, have amounted to from $200,000,000 to $250,000,000 annually.
I think last year it was higher still.
Our new production of gold has also been a matter of great importance to us. Although we have not been on the gold standard since 1929 in the sense of maintaining a free market for gold, we have been obliged to meet in terms of gold the external payments referred to Our production of gold last year was $55,000,000 and the present rate of production is ab9ut $5,000,000 a month. You can realize how important this has been to us.
That was the statement made by myself at the meeting of the imperial economic conference here. Bear in mind that the United States had not then gone off the gold standard, and we had to service our obligations in terms of our contracts or be defaulters-and we were not defaulters for a single dollar. That is worth keeping in mind. At the present time the Minister of Finance has no difficulty such as that. The United States has gone off the gold standard, and the situation is no longer that of our having to find yellow metal, in the language of my friend from Ontario, with which to meet the obligations that arise in respect of provincial or federal securities. That situation has passed away. But we had to do that. We had to do whatever could be done to reduce that discount on Canadian dollars from twenty-five to ten, to eight, to seven, to six per cent; in- 1933 we got it down to 98i cents on the dollar, and thought we had been exceedingly fortunate. That situation is no longer burdening the government of Canada; that situation has been relieved by the action taken in the United States of America. And I should like here to do something I have always longed to do, to say that when England went off the gold standard and our difficulties were very acute, the president of the United States, Mr. Hoover, sent me word saying anything he could do within the limits of his constitutional rights to assist us, he would do, because we had declared that we would meet our obligations in the terms of our contracts-and we did. That is the side to which I draw attention.
Under these circumstances we believed it essential, as we still do, that this country should have a central bank. We believed it for reasons that I will not analyse at the moment. I had in the back of my head the idea, which apparently was not sound because our population was too small, that we might be able to do something with respect to exchange between Great Britain and Canada and not do it through New York; that we might be able through our central banks to establish our own exchange system throughout the countries that constitute the empire, with the central banks of Australia, New Zealand, Great Britain and South Africa. But our population is too small and our volume of business too limited as compared with the tremendous business of New York for us to hope to be able yet to establish clearly-I say, clearly-our position with respect to exchange.

At any rate, that is the position we found in 1933. I was going on to point out that in dealing with this problem of exchange we had one of the most difficult of all the problems that confront any government. For here were these maturities of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, payable in New York in gold; here were the maturities of our country, for instance the renewal of deposits with the Chase National bank,-and I do not forget, either, their great consideration for us at that time of peril and danger. I met the directors and told them exactly what the position was, and what we were striving to do, and they said, "Certainly, if you are trying to do that to meet your obligations, we will renew your obligations", and they did so on what was regarded at that time as most favourable terms. One should at least pay a tribute to those who have endeavoured to help in times of great stress and strain and have done what they could within the limits of their powers, having regard to their constitutional limitations, for the purpose of giving us assistance.
Then we established our central bank; and that was a slow process. Some people think it is a very simple thing to pass a statute. I explained the other day what the difficulties were. The deputy governor said last night in an address he made in this city that the government did what apparently he thinks it is the duty of a government to do,-to appoint a governor and take his advice. At least that is his statement that is printed in the press this morning. That was done, and when this government came into office what did they find? They found a well-equipped, well-officered and manned central bank operating in every province in Canada. They found more. They found not only the original set-up but that the provisions that had been made with respect to treasury bills had been so expanded that from 105 millions they had gone up progressively to 150 millions, where they now stand.

During 1936-
That is what I am talking about, the year after the present government came into office.
During 1936 the amount of dominion government treasury bills outstanding was increased from 105 millions to 150 millions. The average tender rate during the year was -85 per cent for 90-day bills. The rate ranged from 1-198 per cent on the offering of January 2, 1936, to a low of -643 per cent on September 15, 1936, and the last offering of the year was sold at a rate of -746 per cent.
He then points out the difficulty of having any wide market for treasury bills, because bills of that kind in this country are, or were until the offering was made during these five years, an unknown thing. The only dealing with bills had been through the operations of the Finance Act, which by no extension of meaning could be said to be a market for bills in the sense in which that term is used in England.
One word more about that phase of it. The effect of these efforts was to place machinery functioning in every part of this dominion at the disposal of the incoming government. The United States had gone off the gold standard. That trouble had disappeared. Our funds were substantially at par. and if we maintained our trade balances they could be kept there.

That is the position with respect to the matter at the moment. The only construction that I can place upon it is that the minister meant that the banks would be practically out of business so far as note issue is concerned by 1945. Well, the Liberal government did not provide that. In the revision of the Bank Act it is provided that on the first day of January, beginning with 1936, the banks shall retire five per cent of their note issue, and after the next five years, on the first day of January retire ten per cent per annum. That leaves twenty-five per cent of bank notes in Canada and elsewhere in 1945; and I should like the house to keep in mind the "elsewhere." I suppose it is known to every member that there are a number of branches of Canadian banks abroad, and by statute we authorize the issue of paper money in the West Indies by some of our Canadian banks. speechtext:
A base on a strike, yes. The real truth is that we had demand loans at that time for $807,279,133 and investments for $1,440,435,948, a total of $2,247,715,081, or $1,000,000 less than deposits. The business of banking consists in the maintenance of equilibrium between time loans and time deposits, demand loans and demand deposits; and for the purpose of preserving that equilibrium beyond question a cash reserve is set up, which in this case consists of Bank of Canada notes in the hands of the banks and deposits in the Bank of Canada that can be converted into Bank of Canada notes. That may consist of eight, ten, seven per cent or whatever you will of the deposits, but in practice it has been found ample to meet the situation. Why? Because our bankers have thus far been careful enough to maintain that equilibrium between time loans and time deposits and demand loans and demand deposits, so that there has been no claim made upon the cash reserve which exists for the purpose of maintaining the solvency of the institution. The other day I referred to the Merchants' bank, the Union bank, the Northern Crown bank, the Traders' bank, and other institutions that had not maintained that equilibrium between the loans and time deposits. For instance, one of these banks in my own community had lent to a real estate agent several hundreds of thousands of dollars. The boom burst, and where was that money?
The deposit-where was that? Unrealizable. Instead of talking about ten times or eight times, or any other number of times, people should keep in mind the fact that the management is what determines the value of the bank; the administration maintains that high principle of an adjustment between time loans and time deposits and demand loans and demand deposits.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: How are the deposits, created, then?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The deposits are created usually ,by someone writing on a deposit slip and handing so much money into the bank or discounting a piece of paper; that is the reason that Mr. McKenna made the statement that every loan creates a deposit. It does only if the deposit is made in the bank; if it is put elsewhere, in a safety box, or somewhere else, it does not create a deposit.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Why should anyone draw a thousand dollars out of the bank and carry that money around in his pocket and pay interest on it?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: It frequently happens that substantial sums are carried about. Loose money is put away in the cupboard or somewhere else in the home for various purposes. All moneys do not go on deposit in the bank.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: But it has to go back to the bank in interest.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The question of interest does not arise here.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: It does.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The question at the moment is the maintenance of that equilibrium that I have already referred to. There are two kinds of deposits. In the first place you have notice deposits, that is to say, deposits that cannot be withdrawn from the bank unless notice is given to the bank. Loans are made for three months, six months, nine months and so on. but they must be so adjusted that when a man draws a cheque against his account he will find that cheque honoured. And if there comes a time when such a cheque is dishonoured then the bank has failed.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman say that the banks of Canada are safer and stronger than the banks of England? In 1914 when there was a run on the banks of England they did not have the amount of the deposits in cash.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I have told in this chamber once before the story of the difficulties in England. It is difficult to induce

Use oj Canada's Financial Resources
some hon. gentlemen who have very strong views to listen to the facts. The truth is that England was then on the gold standard. The Bank of England did not fail because it had not paper money; it failed because it could not provide gold to exchange for paper money. That is the story.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That is not true of 1914, the year to which the hon. member refers.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I am talking about the failure of the Bank of England. And what is more, I have never listened to a tale' about an inanimate thing that was more moving than the tale of the failure of the Bank of England.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That was not 1914?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: No, this is the failure of the Bank of England, when they had to close as described by the late Chancellor Snowden.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I think the question was as to 1914.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Yes, I was referring to 1914.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Would the right hon.
gentleman say that there is any difference between the pound sterling of to-day and the Bradburys of 1914-15? Neither is backed by gold, and that is the only thing of which there could possibly be any difference.
fMr. Bennett.]

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I have no intention of engaging in a controversy that would lead nowhere. I say they were backed by gold, and I say that the Bank of England has more gold to-day than it ever had at any time in its history, and is carrying it at $20.67 an ounce and not $35. While the currency is not backed by legislation making it technically gold standard money, there was never a time in the history of England when its currency was more fully backed by gold than it is to-day. Anyone who reads the financial newspapers or the last return of the Bank of England will know that. Why try to delude people with a specious story which has no foundation in fact or logic? Why endeavour to cover an issue up by vain words that mean nothing, when as a matter of fact the very money about which the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard is speaking is covered by gold to an extent that it never was covered before in the history of England?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Can they cover the deposits with gold at the present time?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Was there ever a time when the deposits could be covered with gold in any country? Everyone knows what the position is. In the long experience of mankind, by sound judgment and intelligent discretion people have learned to ascertain the likelihood of a run, the likelihood of men demanding their money all at once. I remember during the five years to which I referred one of our banks was suddenly confronted with a run for $10,000,000 because of certain rumours, and they handed out their bills and met the demands promptly and proudly. Under our law as it stands there is no chance of any difficulty arising as long as that is done, because we are the only country in the world that has so favourable an arrangement by reason of the issue of these bills in the terms in which we issue them, as I pointed out the other day. Why endeavour to create a suspicion in the minds of the people that something rotten is being done with respect to these institutions that we ourselves have created? In nine cases out of ten you will find the difficulty arises because someone wants a credit he cannot get. Someone wants to borrow money and cannot; that is what is the matter. Hon. members of this house have said to me: Why cannot I borrow so and so from the bank? I shall never forget a gentleman from Claresholm complaining to me that one of our chartered banks would not lend him money. I said: "Yes, I have a few dollars in that bank; I have an account there. They

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
will not lend that money to you? What have you got?" "Well," he said, "I did have a quarter-section, 'but I sold it, and I have not got much-well, I haven't anything to speak of at all." "Listen," I said; "I would not lend my money to you with any hope of getting it back, and now you are complaining because someone who has control of my money for the moment will not lend it to you. If he did lend it to you I should like to have him dismissed." Did it ever occur to hon. gentlemen that that is the whole story?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: But the hon. gentlemen in the corner do not intend that money borrowed shall ever be paid back.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I listened with my own ears to Mr. Aberhart saying just that on the radio on Sunday night, and dozens of other hon. members doubtless heard it. I do not know whether the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) heard it.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: As a matter of fact I prefer to attend church. I prefer to take mine undiluted. But this is made a catchword amongst our friends in the country-"Oh, look at those banks! They can buy securities or lend ten times their cash reserves!" And someone thinks that means all the money they have on deposit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That is the trouble. But surely my right hon. friend will acquit me of any intention of conveying that impression.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Oh, quite. I would acquit my hon. friend of almost anything in connection with financial matters.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: While we are on that point, if what the right hon. gentleman is now saying is said in earnest, what is the meaning of section 59 of the Bank Act, passed in 1934, which fixes the cash reserve for the merchant bankers at not less than five per cent of the total amount of their deposits? And will he also tell us how much they now have on deposit to support the $2,200,000,000 plus another $600,000,000 on deposit in the banks outside of Canada?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I do not think there is any difficulty about that question, except that it is not quite accurately put. I cannot be both questioner and answerer at the same time, so I shall take the question as though it were accurate and answer it as it should be. The maintenance of the equilibrium between time loans and time deposits and demand loans and demand deposits depends
upon two things. There is the discretion and judgment of the man who is making the loan, whether fifteen, thirty, sixty, ninety or one hundred and twenty days; he has to decide whether notice deposits that he has will be drawn upon within that period, and to what extent. If the notice deposits are not drawn upon-all this is highly technical; he knows it all, has it in front of him-

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: He has it every day.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Yes, I was about to say he had it twice a day, in the larger banks. Therefore he makes his arrangements accordingly. The amount of money is put there as security, in the Bank of Canada or in the gold reserve, and as far as that is concerned my information is that when that is drawn upon to any extent you can be sure that something has gone wrong with the business of the bank.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
What about section 59,
which you wrote into the Bank of Canada Act?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I have not section 59
before me.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Apparently not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
It provides for the
statutory portion of cash reserves required.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That was what I assumed. That is covered at the present moment, Mr. Speaker, by the provisions of our Bank of Canada Act and the Bank Act. To-day our banks have a line of reserve which consists first of Bank of Canada bills and second of deposits in the Bank of Canada, convertible into Bank of Canada bills. Those are the reserves. Those reserves are merely an assurance to the people of the country that their deposits will be safe; that is all.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That a small percentage of them will be safe.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
That is the assurance,
because based upon experience we are able to know that the withdrawals will be so trifling, as against the payment obligations that are provided by loans, that we can rely upon the draft not being made upon them. We all know that. Take your life insurance companies; take your fire insurance companies; take any of your companies. Look at the largest insurance companies in the world; look at the largest in Canada, with outstanding risks amounting to two and a half billion dollars. Why is it perfectly solvent? Because it is based upon those obligations maturing years hence, on an actuarial basis,

computing the interest sometimes at two and a half per cent and sometimes at three per cent, as the case may be; knowing positively as an actuarial matter that some day they will become perfectly complete, and more; more in every case. For instance, there is one company that has $700 of assets for every thousand dollars of insurance outstanding. That is a very old company, needless to say, but that is almost incredible. Of course none of the companies has assets that equals its obligations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Its ultimate obligations.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The obligations on policies, because they are payable in future. The experience of the banks-and I know exactly what I am talking about-is this: every bank-and the older the bank the better- knows what is the likelihood of money being withdrawn. That is a factor of the first importance. For instance, in some parts of the maritime provinces there are savings accounts that have been there for long periods, one of them in particular for three generations. It was willed to somebody, transmitted to the next man and then transmitted to the next. It is one of those old things, a sort of standby; that is all. Those are the notice deposits referred to here. Supposing I go into a bank to-morrow and ask for $10,000. The bank will say, "No, Mr. Bennett, we cannot lend you $10,000." Why? "Because we have reached the end of our lending ability at this moment. In the light of our experience we will be called upon to pay deposits amounting to so much, and we must be in a position to do so."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That does not happen.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Yes, it does. It happened in 1914 in this country, when banks were fearful that maturities would not be paid. It must be remembered that when a bank lends money-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Oh, yes; in a time of crisis.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
That is it, exactly. Just let me put this to this house: A bank predicates its loans upon its knowledge-and I say its knowledge deliberately-gained from experience and otherwise of the likelihood of the obligations being paid in time to enable any claim for deposits to be liquidated. That is the story, shortly put; and when there is a great crisis that interferes with the payments at maturity of course the bank has to take immediate steps to see what can be done to meet the necessities. In England they did it with Bradburys. We did something else, as you will recall, under the war time act 
that dealt with that situation. As far as loans and deposits are concerned the situation must always be this, that banks do not lend more than they have on deposit.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Every loan creates a deposit.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I am quite content that the hon. gentleman has said so, but the misunderstanding on the part of the less intelligent public who listen to a lot of words, such as I have been using, which perhaps they are unable to understand fully, leads to the result that they gather up just a catchword. They say, "By Jove, this bank business must be a terrible thing. There is that bank with its deposits, and it is lending $20,000 on deposits of $2,000." I will tell you that the banks have to deliver just what the deposits call for, and the banks will liquidate their obligations to their depositors in the terms of the deposits. Let there be no misunderstanding about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: We could not have a banking system for five minutes if that were not true.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
It must be true, and that is just why new banks are so difficult to start. In the beginning they have no deposits to deal with, so they start out and lend money to make good fellows of themselves. The next thing that happens is that when my cheque is drawn on that bank I am told that the amount of my deposit is out in a loan that has not been paid, and the bank closes its doors. That is the story.
I am afraid I have gotten far away from what I intended to say-

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Just on that point the right hon. gentleman might give us a little information about the S35,000,000.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Sit down.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
What I should like to point out to the right hon. gentleman is that I did not ask a facetious question. What I wanted to know was why, in the 1934 bank act, the government of that day decided that a five per cent cash reserve was sufficient security against all deposits issued. What has happened is this, that the banks have far more than five per cent of cash on deposit, but in 1934 the government apparently concluded that five per cent of cash was an adequate reserve against deposits in Canadian banks. If that is so the banks can create deposits, as far as the limitations of the law are concerned in Canada, to the extent of $20 for every dollar of cash that they can deposit with the Bank of Canada.

Use of Canada's Financial Resources

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: What was the question?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: My right hon. friend does not need to do that.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: What was the question?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The question is this-

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Why did the government do so and so?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: "The bank act of 1934 sets up a specific quantitative reserve which the chartered banks are required to hold against their deposit liabilities. In form this reserve must consist of a deposit in and notes of the Bank of Canada. In amount it must be equal to five per cent of the deposit liabilities in Canada. As a result the chartered banks as a group can legally create deposits amounting to $20 on the basis of a $1 reserve. A much larger secondary expansion is made possible, however, for the Bank of Canada is required to hold only-"

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I would remind the hon. gentleman that he must ask his question, and that he can interrupt only with the consent of the right hon. gentleman who has the floor.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: My question is: Why did the government decide in 1934 that five per cent was adequate reserve?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I think there were two reasons. One was that this was the amount required in a preceding bank act.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: There was no reserve at all.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: There had been, by practice. There was no central bank, but they had to maintain a reserve in Dominion of Canada bills. That is what the law was. I take it that the hon. gentleman read from that very valuable handbook, McGeer on Progress and Poverty, was it?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I am reading from The Canadian Banking System, by James Holladay, but I can tell my right hon. friend that if he will read that book of mine he will know more than he indicates knowing to-day.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I was mistaken. It was not McGeer on Progress and Poverty he was reading from. But I note with interest his observation that if I read his book I would know more. I always feel we should pay tribute where it is due. He presented me with one. If I were to follow his suggestion and read his book I would know more of what he knew, but I would not know more than I know to-day. It is a very fine distinction.
Let us proceed one step further. The reason why five per cent appeared was this: There was a provision that the banks had to hold Dominion of Canada bills to the extent of a certain sum indicated by statute. Knowing we were to create a central bank, we provided that the reserve should be five per cent. The reason why the five per cent provision was made was threefold. All our banks are not equally strong and, with respect to note issue, the strong have always been careful with respect to the smaller. We have a common fund which takes care of that. It was brought to the attention of the government of that day that a reserve of five per cent had, in the light of experience, been ample. The banks said it had always been and it would always be in excess of five per cent, but they thought that five per cent was sufficient, for statutory purposes, and that as conditions improved-we were then in the depression- it would be competent for them to change that.
As a matter of fact, I believe the banks have averaged since 1934-except at one time, when conditions were extremely bad-between eight per cent and ten per cent. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I think the average would probably be more than ten per cent.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I know it has run over ten per cent, but I am allowing for those dark days when things were lowest. I think it would average something like between eight per cent and ten per cent. It is nearer nine than eight, and I believe the minister might easily give it accurately. But at any rate it has risen, to answer the hon. gentleman's question at once.
In the light of experience it was found that, having regard to maturities and payments by those who borrowed, and in the light of the long time deposits remaining, and the nonfluctuation of them, that reserve would be sufficient to meet any demands which might be made by depositors for their money. In the light of experience that has turned out to be accurate.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Not in every case.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Since the act of 1934 I know of no case in which a depositor has not got his money.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The depositors have not all called for their money at the same time.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
One thing I really delight in is that when a question is answered they merely suggest there was no reason why the
