question should have been asked. I always think that is highly entertaining.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I know of a case.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I said that there was no case since 1934 when the depositor had not been paid; but they say, "No, they did not want their money,'' or in other words, the question should not have been asked.
Banks have very large investments. The minister the other day referred to that fact. It is not from choice, but from necessity, that our banks place their money in securities. Here, for instance, is the central bank's statement for February, in crystallized form, and I find that they have investments of $1,440,435,948. I regret to say that the amount is larger than it was a year ago, and that it is rather larger than it was in January. These are dominion securities, provincial securities, and some municipal, but the one point I want to make clear beyond peradven-ture is that it is a bad sign when banks are compelled to invest their depositors' money in securities. Why?	Because it
indicates a lack of confidence on the part of those who have placed their money in the banks on time deposits, and who are not content to risk it in our industrial and commercial life. I draw an inference there that hon. members opposite will question: That, to me, indicates a lack of confidence. Confidence in this country can be restored only when, with some degree of certainty, men can engage in commercial and industrial enterprises.
At this time we have a trade agreement here, and another trade agreement there. "Shall I expand my plant"? "No; I do not know what is going to happen." " Shall I build a new plant"? "I do not know what is going to happen." "Shall I establish an industry "? " No, I have not confidence that the present situation will continue." I draw an inference my hon. friends opposite will repudiate at once. I say that lack of confidence arises because of the policy of this government; others disagree with that, and that difference of opinion is the foundation of party government. I say that certain things would establish confidence. I say that lack of confidence, non-confidence, is expressed in the central bank's statement, and I think at another time and place I can give very good reasons for so saying.
I have now led up to what I conceive to be the correct conclusion, namely, that we have here a complete lack of confidence, as evidenced by monetary results of policies of the government. One result is an increase in

the securities held by the chartered banks. They have been compelled to increase their holdings of securities, or to refuse to take deposits and pay interest on them, because there is the cost involved in maintaining an office, and in keeping books and records of the deposits themselves. Either one of two things must happen: They have to use that money by investing it, and the investment is of two kinds-loans to customers, or purchases of securities. Investment in a loan is based upon the assumption that the loan at maturity will be paid; that a call upon the reserves will not be made, and that cheques will always be honoured for the deposits of customers. Investment in securities is predicated upon the assumption that during the lifetime of the security nothing will offer for lending purposes, and that therefore it is desirable, yea necessary, that they lock that money up in securities, as is the case. In my judgment, that is an additional signal to this government to take note of the conditions to which I have alluded.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Surely my right hon.
friend will be fair enough to say also that loans, as well as investments, have risen.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Yes; here are the figures. I did not insinuate that they had not risen, and I shall give my figures. A year ago call loans in Canada amounted to $118,000,000. To-day they are $70,000,000. A month ago they were $72,000,000. Those are the figures with respect to call loans.
Ordinary loans, or current loans in Canada have risen $46,000,000 since last year. The amount was $731,456,128, and it has risen $6,000,000 in the last month. It should be observed that the figures are very nearly alike. There is an increase, however, in loans. I do not wish the minister to say that I deny that fact.
I shall not trouble the house further; there is much that could be said, but the diversion which has been offered by the interesting questions which have been asked make it unnecessary to proceed further. The motion to leave the chair was met by an amendment, and the amendment was declared to be a vote of lack of confidence in the government and, as was indicated by the minister at the opening of his speech, was of such a nature that those who were opposed to the government would be disposed to vote for it. But the hon. member's amendment was made a means of suggesting that the alternative proposals of our friends of the social credit group would solve the problem to which they directed attention. That was their position.

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
They talk about monetizing credit. I wonder, sir, how many members of the house have stopped for a moment to think of the extent to which credit has already been monetized in Alberta, and the result of it.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: By past administrations.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Yes; but the credit was monetized to the limit, to such an extent that the interest on that credit could not be met, and default was made in payment of it. In the neighbouring western provinces credit has also been monetized beyond1 the possibility, according to the premiers of those provinces, of their continuing to meet without assistance the obligations thus created. Therefore, when you talk of monetizing credit and of social credit, we know that we have had the monetization of credit in those three provinces and that it has brought about conditions of such a kind that it is unnecessary to do more than merely refer to them as being the answer to the question: Shall there be a further monetization of credit? Of credit, mark you!- of the tar sands and of the Turner valley, of everything connected with the natural resources. All these were pledged when money was borrowed in London. I remember the prospectus of t'he Alberta and Great Waterways issues, and reference will be found there to Alberta's resources. We were monetizing our credit. We did this also in Saskatchewan and in Manitoba. We monetized our credit in every province.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: And now we cannot pay it back.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Precisely, and although we cannot pay it back you want to have more of it.
I shall refer to just one other observation that was made in connection with the amendment, and that had to do with the question of inflation. I am not going to deal this afternoon with the complex and difficult problem of inflation, but I shall just content myself with reading what I said before the board of trade of Toronto in 1933. I said this:
Now I am leaving aside the question as to how you are going to accomplish inflation. I have asked many men for the mechanics of it, and none of them have it except to tell me to borrow perhaps fifty million of dollars, and buy sterling, and perhaps fifty million dollars and buy American exchange, and so manipulate the two as to maintain a stable value for the dollar in terms of the pound. I have had recipes of that kind given me, but they have not said who is going to lend the money or pay the interest.
Then I used these words:
Gentlemen, when you hear people talk about tying the dollar to the pound, I say, from investigations which I made during the last month abroad, we are making ourselves absurd. I use that term deliberately. How are you going to do it? I talked to the foremost authorities in Great Britain, discussed with them the question of inflation in Canada, and do you know what they told me?
And then I said:
This is what he said to me: "Mr. Bennett, in all the history of the world you will find no record of inflation or departure from sound money by any country of its own volition as a matter of deliberate choice. There are two reasons why countries go off sound money, two reasons only when they inflate their currency; one is because of necessity from lack of sound currency and the other insolvency."
These were the reasons given by men who know so much more about this than I shall ever hope to do, that I just give this statement to hon. members as I gave it to my friends in Toronto, for what it may be worth. Certain types of inflation have been going on in these countries all these years. Every thoughtful man knows that. But the type of inflation that has been mentioned in certain of the speeches here, the issue of paper money without regard to-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Debt free money.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Yes. That sort of thing is quite impossible if we are to maintain our solvency. I think everyone realizes that. Professor Ivammener wrote a little volume on money in which he makes this statement which always staggers me, that when German inflation had reached its maximum, a single penny of the United States was sufficient to buy enough marks to discharge the entire mortgage indebtedness of the German empire before the war.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Will the right hon.
gentleman permit a question? I know he would not like to have his statement misconstrued. I should like to point out to him that we did not suggest social credit as a solution. My right hon. friend, if he reads very carefully my remarks, will not find the words "social credit" anywhere. Furthermore, we did not mention setting the printing presses in operation. That statement or meaning was absolutely put into our mouths by other people.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
My mind is quite clear
that the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Blackmore) did not talk of using the printing presses; while he may not have used the words "social credit"-it may have

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
been that it was not desirable to do so-I am bound to say that I could draw nothing else from his remarks, and certainly the theories propounded were what I considered to be an authoritative statement of the principles of social credit. Perhaps I did a wrong to the hon. gentleman in the wording of the subamendment I now propose. I move, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following words:
-but that adoption of the policies of social credit as enunciated by its supporters in this house would afford no adequate remedy for such neglect.
I see no form of amendment by which I can express the lack of confidence in the administration which I have indicated as strongly as I can. At the same time I want to make it quite clear that I have not yet reached that state of intellectual advancement which would enable me to accept the principles enunciated by my friends to the left, with the invaluable assistance of their friend from Vancouver and his work on Progress and Poverty.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue):
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened to a long and rather remarkable speech by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). The subamendment he has just moved is interesting, and if it could be accepted without joining it to the amendment that was moved by the leader of the social credit group (Mr. Blackmore), I have no doubt that we on this side of the house would be prepared to support it. However, support of the subamendment involves the prevention of the house from going into committee of supply, and the subamendment will therefore have to be rejected by the administration along with the amendment that was proposed by the hon. member for Lethbridge. That is the position which I think the government will have to take on this motion.
Coming to the speech of the leader of the opposition, it is a little difficult for me to remember all that the right hon. gentleman has said. He began his speech on the fourteenth day of March; he continued it at considerable length on the twenty-second day of March, and he resumed it to-day. Having in mind that I might possibly wish to follow him I formulated some thoughts two or three weeks ago, but they have become a little vague and hazy at this late date. I have, however, this general impression of his speech as a whole. There were two parts of it that were quite surprising to me. The first was the position taken by the right hon. gentle-
man the other night in reference to a passage he quoted from the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), and in order that there may be no dispute as to what the Minister of Finance said, and as to the position taken by the leader of the opposition in reference to it, I turn to page 1151 of Hansard of March 8, where the Minister of Finance said this:
An increase of, say $350,000,000 in chartered bank holdings of Bank of Canada notes would increase their cash reserves from the present figure of about $250,000,000 to $600,000,000, and their cash ratio from about ten per cent to roughly twenty-one per cent.
The sponsor of the suggestion contends that no inflation is intended or would result by thus increasing bank cash, so long as the gold cover of the Bank of Canada did not fall below the twenty-five per cent minimum. This factor, however, is not a test of inflation. If the banks use their increased cash in the normal way, as a basis for the extension of roughly ten times as much in loans to the public, or for the acquisition of ten times as much in investments, bank deposits would expand by approximately an equal amount until the cash ratio was brought down again to approximately ten per cent. This would mean an increase in bank deposits from the present level of about $2,387,000,000 to something like $6,000,000,000, or more than 2-6 times the level of December 31, 1929. Am I merely old fashioned or orthodox when I say that this would mean a colossal measure of inflation?
The right hon. gentleman challenged that statement very sharply; in fact he characterized part if not all of it as "monstrous nonsense"; and because of the position taken by him, I think I should make clear what I believe is the true position. I believe, and I think most hon. members have believed for some years, that generally speaking it is true that loans create deposits, that is to say, that loans made by banks find their way immediately either into accounts in the same bank or into accounts in other banks, and that therefore loans are responsible for, result in, lead to, create deposits. The right hon. gentleman challenged that statement, and challenged it sharply. He put forward the case of a borrower from a bank who puts the money in his pocket and neither puts it in the bank himself nor gives it to anybody who directly or indirectly puts it in a bank. The simple answer to that is the one given this afternoon by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Landeryou) in his question, that that is beyond the range of the normal experience of human beings. Human beings may hoard money; but they do not hoard money on which they are paying interest, and the amount of hoardings of borrowed moneys would be infinitesimal, so small a factor in the whole situation that it cannot seriously be advanced as a reason for challenging the

Use oj Canada's Financial Resources
broad general statement, now commonly accepted, that loans do create deposits.
As a matter of fact, there is the best of authority for this statement. I suppose that the highest authority in the English speaking world to-day is that of the committee on finance and industry, which was made up of some of the greatest monetary economists and practical bankers in the world. The chairman of this committee was the Right Hon. H. P. Macmillan, K.C. The right hon. gentleman would not challenge his authority; he himself selected Mr. Macmillan to head a commission in Canada which investigated the banking situation in this country. I desire to read at this time two or three sections of this report so that the matter may be clearly understood. A great many hon. members, in speaking to me about the speech of the right hon. gentleman the other evening, said that he was right; that his position was sound. But his position is unsound and incorrect, as is shown by the report of the Macmillan commission. I shall read two paragraphs only, although several others also bear out the position that I am taking at the moment. Paragraphs 74 and 75 put the position absolutely clearly.
74. It is not unnatural to think of the deposits of a bank [DOT] as being created by the public through the deposit of cash representing either savings or amounts which are not for the time being required to meet expenditure.
That I take to be the position of the right hon. gentleman the other evening.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: No. I made it perfectly clear that a loan created a deposit, and I quoted McKenna to-day to the same effect.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman quoted McKenna only to criticize him.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: No; I admit that a loan creates a deposit if it is deposited in a bank.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I will admit, Mr. Speaker, that the passage which was quoted the other night was not represented as "monstrous nonsense" to-day. The right hon. gentleman took an entirely different position to-day.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: No, he did not.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: And with nearly everything he said to-day I am in agreement.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Well, then, we shall have a dumping duty shortly.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I do not want anyone
reading Hansard of the other evening to conclude that there is something in the position he took on that occasion, and therefore-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
The minister does not agree with the tariff utterances of the right
hon. gentleman to-day, but agrees with his monetary references.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Yes; as has been suggested, I want to make it clear that it is with his monetary references that I am in agreement, and not with his statements about adverse balances and favourable balances of trade, to which I shall refer.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The minister will get there, too.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That assumes that all the deposits are made in one bank. It does not take into consideration that deposits are made in other banks or that deposits are made in other banks in other countries.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Well, then, I shall read paragraph 75:
75. The process is much the same when we remove the assumption that there is only one bank. The credit granted by one bank may

Use oj Canada's Financial Resources
reach the accounts of customers in another bank. There is thus established a claim by the second bank upon the first for cash, and the ability of the second bank to grant loans is improved in so far as that of the first bank is reduced. Over the banking system as a whole therefore, loans and investments made by the banks increase their deposits. There is, however, a limitation on this process. A bank which is actively creating deposits in this way will naturally find that a considerable part of the cheques drawn against them will be in favour of other banks. It will thus lose part of its cash reserve to those banks and must proceed to limit its loan operations if its normal cash ratio is to be maintained. In practice, therefore, no one bank can afford to pursue a policy of creating deposits by making loans or investments which is much out of line with the policies of other banks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That is exactly what I said the other night.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
It is exactly in line with what the Minister of Finance said in his speech the other night.
I believe there is something in what the right hon. gentleman says to the effect that the statement that loans create deposits may mislead some people. There is something in that position, and I have no quarrel with the warning he gave to the house and to the country this afternoon. It is not true that a bank can lend wildly and indefinitely to any class of borrowers, thereby creating a huge amount of credit money which is put into circulation in the dominion. There are two very well understood limitations upon the power of banks to increase credit money: The first is the necessity of preserving an adequate cash ratio, and that has been fully explained this afternoon. The bank must follow the normal banking practice with regard to the preservation of the cash ratio, and if that ratio is too small, there is danger of the bank being called upon to make payment in cash which it cannot make, with the result that it will find itself in trouble. The second limitation is that the loans must be good loans. The loans and investments must be good. If they are not, then the bank will find that its deposits, which are good deposits created by loans, which are liabilities of the bank, will be in excess of the value of the loans and investments, which are assets of the bank, and the bank will be insolvent and will fail, as the Merchants bank failed. My right hon. friend explained that the other night. The right hon. gentleman did not say frankly that he was wrong the other night, as he might just as well have said this afternoon; but after the explanation he has given us today there is not much difference of opinion between the parties in the house with respect to the true nature of banking operations.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Is it true that the banks of Canada owe the people of Canada between one and two thousand million dollars cash? Have the people that amount on deposit with the banks? That is the first question I should like to ask the minister, and the second is this: If they have that amount, how can the banks pay their obligations to the people if there is less than $300,000,000 cash in the whole dominion?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The answer to the first question is, yes. The banks do owe the people of the dominion something over two billion dollars. The answer to the second question is that so long as the banks maintain an adequate cash ratio, they can pay all that in the ordinary course of events they will ever be called upon to pay. That is the practical way of dealing with the situation, and anything else is merely academic and theoretical.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Does that not prove that the banks do create credit; that a loan does create a deposit?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Everyone admits that. Everyone says so.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Does that not prove that the banks do create money?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I shall answer a reasonable number of questions, but not too many.
Let me now deal with the other statement of the right hon. gentleman, a statement that surprised me. It is not so much a statement, for I do not think I can actually quote it; it is rather the general position he took in reference to adverse and favourable trade balances. Ever since I have been in the house I have heard this matter of adverse and favourable trade balances discussed, and while I am not sufficiently versed in economics or in the theory of international trade to deal at all thoroughly with the position taken by the leader of the opposition this afternoon, I am satisfied that almost any economist would regard with great surprise the touching faith which the right hon. gentleman has in favourable trade balances as a means of enriching a country. The position he has taken seems to be that if we send out more goods and services than we bring in, we are getting rich, and if we bring in more goods and services that we send out, we are getting poor; and that at all costs we must preserve a substantial trade balance.
My understanding is that over a period of time the amount of goods and services exported balances with the amount of goods and services imported, and if there is a tem-

Use oj Canada's Financial Resources
porary trend in one direction or the other, the effect on the currency is very likely to operate powerfully to restore the balance. For instance, if we were to export very heavily in proportion to our imports, there would be a demand by the purchasers of our exports for our exchange, which would cause our exchange to appreciate in terms of the exchange of the countries in which the persons buying our goods live; and when that happens, an adverse influence is set up against our exports. The same is true if we import excessively in proportion to our exports. For the time being there is likely to be a depreciation in our currency, which in turn will encourage exports.
I am sure the leader of the opposition when he came into power in 1930 did not start out consciously to affect the value of our currency by his dumping duties and high tariffs. I followed closely the course of events in those years. I was in this house in opposition, and I think the records will bear me out when I say that his object in raising the tariffs and imposing dumping duties to the exorbitant degree that he did upon goods coming into Canada was to end unemployment-to give work to the people of the country. That is what he said at the time.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That was one object.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: We did not hear anything about currency for two or three years.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
The records are there. The predominant motive, the reason given for the imposition of the dumping duties, was to give work to Canadian citizens-an object which, by the way, did not succeed-and it was not until people became interested in currency matters in 1932 and 1933 that the right hon. gentleman, ex post facto, took credit for having previously looked into the matter and taken steps to maintain our currency. It is an open question whether the maintenance of our currency at the level at which it stood in those years was a good or a bad thing for the country. I always felt, despite the argument to which we have listened this afternoon, that our currency for two or three yeare during that period was maintained at too high a level, though I admit that there are two views in that regard. As the leader of the opposition said, we were caught between the pound sterling and the United States dollar. As regards certain of our interests, it seemed advantageous to maintain our Canadian dollar at a high level so as to permit those of our municipalities and industries
which had payments to make in the United States to make them with greater facility than they could otherwise have done. But from the standpoint of our exporters, who are a very substantial part of the population, it would certainly have been advantageous if Canada's dollar had followed the pound sterling to a greater extent than it did.
Now, sir, I want to deal with two or three statements that have been made. One of them has reference to this $3,000,000 loaned to Saskatchewan. I deal with this because tL/_ statements made in the house by the right hon. leader of the opposition-or not so much the statements as the tone in which they were made-seemed to carry the implication of irregularity on the part of the Bank of Canada.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Not the slightest suggestion of irregularity.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Well, they certainly were calculated to disturb public confidence in the Bank of Canada. I say that, having heard the right hon. gentleman on the floor of the house and read his speeches since. I want to refer to that $3,000,000 transaction.
It will be remembered that these loans were made by the Bank of Canada in the spring of 1936. There had been a dominion-provincial conference in December, 1935, which continued into January, 1936. The delegates and this government agreed upon the setting up of a system of loan councils, that is an individual loan council for each province.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Each of the provinces which desired it.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Yes. The essential feature of the loan council scheme was that borrowing and financing generally by the provinces which came into the scheme would be under the control of the dominion government. It was contemplated that there would be a refunding of the obligations of the provinces which came into the scheme. The government undertook to submit to parliament legislation which would establish a loan council scheme. That legislation, or the preliminary resolution necessary for the legislation, was brought into parliament, and if I remember correctly, if, was rejected by the senate. But before the legislation was so rejected, and while the Bank of Canada thought, and had reason to think, that a loan council scheme or system was coming into existence, the Bank of Canada made these loans to Saskatchewan, believing that they were making temporary loans. On May 1, 1936, a four and a half per cent bond issue of Saskatchewan, in the amount of

$2,000,000, was to mature. As the old peace, order and good government legislation had expired on March 31, 1936, the dominion government had no power to make a loan to the province to meet this impending maturity. maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
That is April 30. I
thought the minister said the loan was not made until May 1.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Then the bank still held the securities. That is what I want to know.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
It is apparent, therefore, that the two loans were made as advances for six months under section 21 (1) (k) of the Bank of Canada Act, which section also provides that this type of loan must be repaid before the end of the first quarter after the
rMx. Ilsley.]
end of the fiscal year of the provincial government concerned. It is obvious that what the bank had in mind was that within the six months' period the loan council legislation would have been passed and an arrangement completed for refunding the outstanding debt of Saskatchewan as contemplated by the loan council legislation. Had this happened, the bank's loan to the province would have been paid off at maturity as a result of the refunding operation. However, as hon. members know, the loan council legislation failed of passing in the senate, and consequently the province had no means of finding the cash with which to pay off the $3,000,000 owing to the Bank of Canada. The bank's weekly statements show, therefore, that at the maturity of the loans the bank took the province's treasury bills. Is that not the whole story?

speechtext: It was all tabled in the house. It is no mystery.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I want to deal with the question of publicity, because if there was ever a transaction to which the fullest publicity was given it was this transaction. It was thoroughly publicized in this house and out of it.
In the budget speech of May 1, 1936, the Minister of Finance referred to this loan. He said:	[DOT]
The province of Saskatchewan, which has an issue maturing to-day, May 1, has expressed a willingness to participate in the loan council

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
arrangement and with the understanding that the dominion will proceed with its legislation the province, 1 am advised, has made arrangements with the Bank of Canada to enable it to meet this maturity.
Then on June 18, 1936, a return was tabled in the house giving copies of the correspondence exchanged between this government and the government of Saskatchewan in regard to the loan to be obtained by the province from the Bank of Canada.
The third time that the matter was referred to in the house was the next year, on April 10, 1937. The minister had been moving the second reading of Bill No. 118, for granting to His Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending March 31, 1938, and after the leader of the opposition had made a statement in connection with this same loan to the province of Saskatchewan, the Minister of Finance made a statement in regard to the whole matter. I do not think it is so long that I should not read it. It may be found on page 2941 of Hansard for 1937.
So we said there would he no more advances to enable any province to meet maturing obligations.
Sir, we applied this policy absolutely and entirely without discrimination. We had applications from all the western provinces. Then, in an attempt to meet the situation, the dominion-provincial conference came to the unanimous decision to adopt a modified loan council idea, and they had our assurance that we would place the matter before parliament. While that process was going on maturities took place in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, and I think a small one in Manitoba. It seemed to us that anything that could be done to anticipate the coming into force of the then contemplated loan council legislation, in order to prevent any of these provinces from being the first among Canadian provinces to default, would be worth while. But of course in order that it might be effective the province concerned necessarily had to consent to take advantage of the loan council plan.	British Columbia said, no;
British Columbia got no advance to meet its maturity. Alberta said, no; Alberta got no advance to meet its maturity. Manitoba said, yes, conditionally; we were not in a position to accept conditions, and Manitoba got no assistance. Saskatchewan said, yes, we will go in. But by the time they said yes, this government had no authority from this parliament to loan money for that purpose. The old peace, order and good government legislation had expired and we had no authority. They went to the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of Canada, without being prompted by this government in the slightest degree-in fact I had no knowledge of the initial negotiations- expressed a willingness to advance the money to save default, provided it had satisfactory assurance from the government of Saskatchewan that it would introduce the necessary
provincial legislation to enable that province to enter the loan council scheme, and provided that the bank had assurance from the government of Canada that it intended to proceed with the loan council scheme. Saskatchewan gave the necessary assurance. Naturally we also gave the assurance, and the funds were advanced to Saskatchewan by the Bank of Canada to meet that maturity. Were it not for that particular instance there would be no question of misunderstanding between the leader of the opposition and myself. To him the history of that transaction involves discrimination against the other western provinces. To me it does not, because I have been conscious of nothing throughout this whole difficulty more than a desire to treat each of those provinces absolutely equitably. When I say equitably, I do not mean equally. Equal treatment is impossible. Equitable treatment is possible, and I maintain has been extended by this government since we came into office. What do I mean by equitable treatment? I mean the establishment of a principle which is available to all, which applies equally to all, and which depends for its working upon acceptance by each.
The right hon. gentleman went further in his speech the other night and made an attack on the changes which were made in the form of the weekly statement of assets and liabilities of the Bank of Canada. He made a strong point of that and dealt with it at considerable length, and I want to reply to what he had to say.

The right hon. gentleman said that was a wrong thing to do, because the public ought to know how much the bank had invested in sterling and how much it had invested in United States dollars. But there is a good reason why the public should not know that. The reason is just this, that speculators in these exchanges, studying the operations of the Bank of Canada and seeing that they were going out of sterling into United States dollars or going out of United States dollars into sterling, as the case might be, were in a position to get knowledge of the opinion of the Bank of Canada as to the trend or probable trend of these currency markets. That was the reason. To leave those separated as they were would be to give the speculators something by which they could guide their operations and anticipate transactions. That was the reason, and the only one.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT

The purpose is set out in the preamble of the act, and it is not an information bureau for speculators, whether they are business men or anybody else. That was what it tended to be, with the other heading.

It read, "Reserves in funds of other countries on a gold standard," which might have implied that sterling was a gold standard currency. As the bank had hitherto held no discounts, did not anticipate having any, and still has none, it was thought unnecessary to subdivide this item until need should arise. I do not know whether or not the right hon. gentleman attacked that, but that was the reason for the change.
The fifth change was this: It had been observed that should the Bank of Canada make an advance to one of the Quebec savings banks, which was possible under the act, there was no place under heading No. 4 where it could be entered. The heading was therefore altered from " Chartered banks " to " Chartered and savings banks." Under item No. 6, " Investments," one item was made of all dominion and provincial government short term securities.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: So we are no longer able to know what advances are made to the provinces.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Quite. That is the point the right hon. gentleman stressed the other night, perhaps I should say with a rather sinister accent.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: This is the first time accents have been the subject matter of discussion in parliament.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: This change was considered advisable, as otherwise if only one province were borrowing from the bank at one time, as indeed would be the usual case, the affairs of that province might receive undesirable publicity. I want to point out that the right hon. gentleman was trying to leave the impression the other night, and I think he stated in so many words, that the change was made to cover up this transaction.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The statement just made' indicates that to be so.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Not at all, because this-transaction was given the fullest publicity' six months before, as well as later. I have given the three respects in which this parliament was given full information as to this particular transaction, so this change could not have been made to hide that transaction. I think that follows. I suppose if we had a large transaction in the future, an important transaction such as this, the same publicity would be given to it; but if the Bank of Canada reached the position where it was making small loans or frequent loans to the provinces, is it in the public interest that the other provinces which are dealing with the bank should know what the financial transactions are between the Bank of Canada and the provinces? They certainly do not have it now when they go to a commercial bank.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The Bank of Canada declined to do anything for Ontario, and the very point I make is just what the minister has said, that it enabled this to be covered up. maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
It was given the fullest publicity; therefore that could not be the motive or reason. The point is that the charge against the bank, that the bank did this to cover up something, certainly is not borne out by the record. The bank considers that in the matter of publicity, as in so many other things, moderation should be the objective. It considers that the present form of the bank return meets all reasonable requirements. Indeed, even in its present form the return probably discloses as much, if not more, information in regard to the bank's operations than is the case in any other central bank in the world.

But in regard to control and the power to direct policy, the power to map out a policy for the Bank of Canada, there has been all the difference in the world.
I want to point out three respects in which our banking legislation differs from his. The first is that the government now owns 51 per cent of the stock, and thereby assumes voting control. The second is this: Under his administration the directors were selected by the shareholders. Now the majority of the directors is nominated by the government, and the arrangement is such that at all times the government directors have a complete majority over the other directors, and the governor and deputy governor of the bank. So that the bank is at all times under the control of the government appointed directors. That is the second respect-

14. No action or decision of the board of directors, or of the executive committee, shall have any effect unless the same is concurred in by the governor, or in his absence or incapacity, by the deputy governor.

maintopic: NIAGARA FALLS OBSERVATION BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while perhaps it would be better for me to make my observations on the third reading of this bill, I shall take only four or five minutes tonight. The principle of this bill has been before the house on nine different occasions, from 1923 to 1935 when other bridge bills were before us. I am not opposing the principle of this bill. I am in favour of the principle of public ownership of bridges of this kind between the state of New York and the province of Ontario. They should be publicly owned and publicly controlled. When the Sarnia bridge bill came before the house, Sir Henry Thornton was represented before the committee and proposed that the Canadian National Railways should have the ownership and control of all such international undertakings as feeders for this railway. The
Niagara Falls Bridge

Niagara district is one of our great tourist districts, and that great park of the Niagara parks commission stretching from lake Erie to lake Ontario, with all the future bridges between the state of New York and the province of Ontario, should be publicly owned and controlled, and free of tolls as a gesture of good will and an aid toward friendly relations. It is a great credit to the government of Sir Oliver Mowat that started that great park; that he bought all that land and developed it as a park, and under the chairmanship of the late Mr. P. W. Ellis the parks commission went ahead and did a great development work for many years, now extended very well by the present government.
I should like to hear from the sponsor of this bill whether there will be any variation from the principle I have described of public ownership in connection with this bridge. I attended a meeting of the railway committee and there was considerable discussion over this bill. Notwithstanding what was said the day before in this house about a lobby, I saw the biggest lobby I have ever seen before the committee when this bill was being considered. I should like to know if the principle of public ownership is going to be preserved in connection with this bridge or will the bridge be handed over or leased later on to somebody else? Will the government have absolute control over the rates and tolls? For fifteen years I have contended for public ownership of all these bridges in connection with the nine similar bills that have been before this house. The tourist traffic in the Niagara district is becoming so great, with a continual flow of motor cars crossing, that I do not know how it is going to be handled. I admit that the present Ontario government deserve credit for the way in which they have developed that area, and the Conservative government before them did some good work under Mr. Ellis, as chairman of the parks commission, so there is enough credit to go all around.
I do not like the hide-and-go-seek features of this bill. We had several bills for bridges across the St. Lawrence at various places, and one at Sarnia, and another at Windsor, and in my opinion it would be far better if New York state and the Ontario government built this bridge, and owned, controlled and operated it. When one sees the cars lined up at the Peace bridge, waiting to pass the customs and immigration inspectors, would it not be better if this new bridge would be free of tolls? It is different with the tourist traffic at Lewiston and Queenston on the steamer Cayuga, because the passengers can pass through Lewiston or

Queenston in a minute or two, but the congestion on the Peace bridge is intolerable from inspection of customs and immigration officers. Both governments should cooperate in building and owning and controlling this bridge, and free it of tolls. It affords the greatest opportunity that I know of for a demonstration of good will between the two countries. The government of Ontario have spent a lot of money well and some foolishly, but undoubtedly on the whole they have done very good work in the Niagara Falls district, and the Niagara parks commission deserves great credit. The promoter of this bill has no doubt given a great deal of study to the question, and I should like to know from him whether this property will be handed over for construction and operation to the Niagara parks commission and whether the rights of the city of Niagara will be preserved, so that there will be no abuse of this legislation.
On the other bills to which I made reference earlier in my remarks were Bill No. 42, to-incorporate the Port Huron-Sarnia bridge in 1928; Bill No. 79, incorporating the Niagara Falls memorial bridge in 1927, and Bill No. 22 of the same year, I took the same stand, and by the way I might say that some of the other bridge franchises were peddled all over the north American continent, and in Wall street and among the banks, the franchises were for sale after they had been secured from parliament. All Ontario governments of both parties have done splendid work in connection with the development of the Niagara park area since it was created by the government of Sir Oliver Mowat in the late eighties. The tourist traffic is going to develop by leaps and bounds with the-popularity of the motor car, and in my opinion there should be no tolls at all on the bridge. Tolls are just a relic of the ox-cart days. The bridge should be publicly owned and controlled in the interests of the people. This parliament has control of all bridges that are international, interprovincial, or that affect navigation. If we have all the necessary safeguards now in the bill, I shall not oppose it.
We cannot visualize the future traffic that will go over that bridge with the development of the motor bus. The steamboat business is not what it used to be; they have only one boat the Cayuga, on that river; at the-other end of lake Erie conditions are a little better. I am bound to say that I believe the hon. gentleman will find that, we are doing something for which we have no legal warrant. I am perfectly aware of what he has pointed out with respect to other companies and what has been done with them. One related to a tunnel, the other three to bridges. We had occasion to point out to some of the gentlemen who were interested that they would have some difficulty in dealing with this; and if the hon. gentleman will look at the preamble of the bill-it has not yet been passed, but I may be permitted to refer to it-they have prayed for the right to construct and maintain and operate a bridge across the Niagara river into the city of Niagara Falls in the state of New York. It is perfectly clear and does not require any argument from a lawyer to point out that this parliament cannot give anyone power to build a bridge in New York state. The second point is that section 8 in its terms purports . to do that very thing. That is the section now under consideration.
8. The company may construct, maintain and operate a bridge across the Niagara river-
After it gets to the centre of the stream it is in the United States territory.
-for the passage of pedestrians, vehicles, carriages, electric cars, street cars and other like purposes with all necessary approaches, roads and works, from a point between a point north of the present Upper Steel arch bridge and the north limit of Bender street in the city of Niagara Falls, in the county of Welland, in the province of Ontario, to a point in the city of Niagara Falls in the state of New York, one of the United States of America, north of the present upper steel arch bridge, and may purchase, acquire and hold such real estate, including lands for sidings and bridge heads and other equipment required for the convenient working of traffic to, from and over the said bridge as the company thinks neces-

sary for any of the said purposes; but the company shall not commence the actual construction of the said bridge nor exercise any of the powers hereunder, until an act of congress of the United States or other competent authority in the United States of America has been passed authorizing or approving such bridging of the said river, but the company may, in the meantime acquire the lands, submit their plans to the governor in council and do all things authorized by this act.
I submit to the Minister of Justice that it is quite clearly beyond our powers here; and all the others have been in exactly the same position. I can clearly recall the authorities, but I am not going to weary the committee with discussions of that sort. Surely, however, we must not endeavour to exceed our legislative jurisdiction with respect to an international matter. When, in 1935, the time for completion of the Sarnia bridge was being extended, the language used was quite clear:
The construction of the said subway or tunnel shall be commenced within one year after the governor in council and the executive of the United States of America have approved . . .
Under this measure the governor in council is to approve the plans, and that is all. But how can the governor in council approve plans for the state of New York? The matter should be faced frankly. There is no getting away from it that we are exceeding our legislative jurisdiction in what we are doing, and it will be only a nullity when it is encountered in reality.

interest. We are now in the position where there is a difference between a public authority and the owners of the old structure; therefore I would move that the bill be recommended.

"I think Hon. McQuesten is reading into that resolution a meaning that was never intended." his worship said. Reiterating the statement he has made several times since the Falls View bridge collapsed, Mayor Hanniwell said he didn't care who builds the bridge, so long
as it is erected as quickly as possible, and this city receives taxation from the span and its property.

I want now to quote from a celebrated authority on social credit, no less than Major Douglas himself, and I shall give the reference to his work. This is what he says in his book Social Credit, revised edition, chapter 2, page 94:
In the foregoing chapter rve have endeavoured to establish two important propositions in generalized terms. The first of these is:

I now quote from the Monopoly of Credit by Major Douglas, pages 106 and 107:
A factory or other productive organization has besides its economic function as a producer of goods, a financial aspect-it may be regarded on the one hand as a device for the distribution of purchasing power to individuals, through the media of wages, salaries, and dividends; and on the other hand as a manufactory of prices-financial values.
From this standpoint its payments may be divided into two groups:
Group A-All payments made to individuals (wages, salaries, and dividends).
Group B-All payments made to other organizations (raw materials, bank charges, and other external costs).
Now the rate of flow of purchasing power to individuals is represented by A, but since all payments go into prices, the rate of flow of prices cannot be less than A plus B. Since A will not purchase A plus B, a proportion of the product at least equivalent to B must be distributed by a form of pur-51952-116-
chasing power which is not comprised in the description grouped under A.
I am merely placing on record these extracts from the writings of Major Douglas. I shall leave it to any member of this house, if he will read the speech of the Minister of Finance, and then read this, as to whether the minister did not accurately, precisely, fairly and fully state Major Douglas' A plus B theorem. Anyone coming into the house to-day and' listening to the discussion that we have been hearing would wonder what was the question before the house, and therefore I think it would be just as well to read again the motion presented by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore):
That all the words in the motion after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefore: "This house is of the opinion that for the effective removal of poverty from Canada this government has neglected and is now neglecting to use the resources of the dominion as adequately as the people of this country have a right to demand."
It is that motion which I want to discuss for a short while this evening. I am satisfied that the motion is timely and that it is for the government to prove that they are meeting the requirements of the Canadian people. This resolution no doubt springs out of the promises which were made by the present government prior to the election. I take it that every citizen of Canada has around him the evidence to satisfy himself whether those pledges have been carried out and whether this resolution is timely or not. I believe I am safe in saying that a large majority of the Canadian people believe there is something wrong with the present situation, which has produced the condition in which we find, ourselves to-day. The evidence is manifest; throughout the country. Some of us cart go back a number of years and compare conditions, say thirty years ago, with conditions to-day. Thirty years ago there was a song of joy and gladness everywhere in the country; optimism characterized the people who went, to build homes for themselves and their little ones, and to establish a future for the dominion. Compare that with the condition in which we

Over the radio two weeks ago on Sunday night the ex-president of the board of trade speaking from Montreal with regard to the funded debt of Canada said that it was around eight billion dollars. That means for each person a debt of S800. At confederation that per capita debt stood at $21.87. I ask you, sir, whether there is not something seriously wrong with a system which creates a condition like that in these few years. In the speech by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in response to that of the hon. member for Lethbridge, he said that this government had control sufficient for the needs of the people. I quote his words, as found at page 1146 of Hansard:
Canada's financial machinery is now adequate to enable the government to cause effective action to be taken in the field of monetary policy to the extent that monetary methods may be appropriate to solve our problems.
That is quite an acknowledgment to make. The government recognizes that it has at the present time the machinery to solve the country's problems. That is what this resolution calls upon the government to do. The question is, Is there evidence that they are doing it? The Minister of Finance said also:
It should be noted also that Canadian deposits -and, mark you, these represent the credit which does ninety to ninety-five per cent of the money work of Canada-are now at a level nearly twenty-two per cent above the figure for October 31, 1932, and over $117,000,000 higher than at the end of the boom year 1929.
Again he said, as reported on page 1148:
TFinally, chartered bank deposits with the central bank and their holdings of Bank of Canada notes have risen by $41,000,000. This latter total is the increase in bank cash which has made possible an expansion of over $350,000,000 in Canadian bank deposits or Canadian credit during that period of two and three-quarter years.
What I am concerned about is, Where is this credit, and is it available for the use of the people of this dominion? Is there any manifestation of its being used? It is useless to create additional credit and leave it in the bank; it is doing no good there. It is a matter of policy if it is not being put to work. There is something wrong with the system that has created the position in which we find ourselves. Since confederation our debt has been enormously increased. If my recol-

lection is correct, $273,000,000 was the federal debt at confederation. Now it has reached over $3,000,000,000. There has been either mismanagement or bad policy. I cannot think this situation is due to mismanagement by the ministers who have been in office since that time; I am inclined to think it is due to the policy that has been followed. There have been both Conservative and Liberal administrations, and in point of time it is about fifty-fifty between them. It could not have been any nearer had it been arranged, and perhaps it was. But it has made little or no difference which party was in power; the results have been the same, because they have both been following the same policy. Lord Salisbury said, "The commonest error in politics is sticking to the carcasses of dead policies."

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That is good Conservative doctrine.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Analyse the situation
as it is to-day, a bonded debt of around $8,000,000,000 with the policy that has been in vogue since confederation, and tell me if there is any hope for the future by following the same policy.
We heard a great deal this afternoon about debt, interest and the accumulation of debt. The statement has been made in the house that 63 cents out of every dollar paid in taxes goes to pay interest. What is going to happen when it takes the whole dollar? That will not be very long, at the rate the debt is increasing. Something will happen then; I do not know what. I am wondering why some people are so anxious to keep the same policy in vogue. If we ask ourselves who they are who are fighting so mightily at the present time to prevent any change in the policy of governments in this country, we shall find that they are those to whom the present system has been very kind.
We heard a good deal this afternoon about loans and bonds. I say with all seriousness that if the credit of this country is good for a dollar bond, it is just as good for a dollar bill. If the credit of the country is good to float a loan of $100,000,000 through financial institutions, it should be just as good to float that loan by the government itself. It seems to me that where we and other parties differ is in regard to the issue and control of the currency and credit of the dominion. I and thousands more in this dominion want to know why the credit of this country in the floating of loans or bond issues must go through financial institutions, so that the people have to be taxed not only for the loan but for the interest that goes with it.

We claim that the floating of loans, the issuing of bonds, should not carry interest whereby the people are burdened with this debt and interest which are growing by leaps and bounds year after year. I have yet to meet one person who holds out any hope at all that our national debt will ever be paid. I should like anyone in the house to tell me if he has any hope that we shall ever pay our national debt, which is growing so rapidly.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: If an annuity were provided, as was provided by statute at one time in Ontario, and if we had been able to escape the depression, an annuity established would have been sufficient to wipe out the debt in the course of about a hundred years; that is, if we had been able to give effect to it.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Why could it not be done?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Depression.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: What caused the depression? War. What caused the war?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I think probably social credit.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: And so it goes on, just one continual round, chasing in a circle. That is just what it amounts to. It is the same to-day; we have the same problems we have had right along. What were the problems facing Canada in 1930? They were unemployment, absence of purchasing power and heavy taxation. What are they in 1938? They are just the same, only we are worse off because our debt and interest have almost doubled in these last few years; not quite doubled, but at least grown very rapidly.

speechtext:
Yes; but that is only a fleabite, and the increase in the debt just about makes up for that. Then the government ask us to have confidence in their policies and to look forward to better times. I have jotted down this statement, referring to unemployment and so on: Idle men willing to work are a disgrace to any government. Idle machines are a serious reflection on our system, and idle money is the greatest curse of all, money which should be in circulation but which is tied up in bank vaults and so on. It should be the most serious concern of the government at this time to find the proper application of men, machines and money to the welfare of mankind in this country. If this government can find that proper application, it will solve the problem. There is a proper application, but I am satisfied that it is out of adjustment at the present

There is no greater tragedy than to see men and women who have lost heart, who feel that they have no place in the scheme of things, in the society in which they move at the present time. There are thousands who have lost heart and many others who are on the border line at the present time. Think of the youth, as compared with the youth of thirty or forty years ago. Think of the outlook we had as boys; compare it with the outlook before the youth of to-day. We planned and worked and studied in order that when we built our homes and raised our families, we might leave them a better heritage than we received. The fathers and mothers are seriously concerned at the present time and are looking to this government for some solution. That is what is dealt with in the Tesolution we are discussing to-night. It is still true, as in former years, that Lazarus waits for the crumbs that fall from the rich man's table.
There are two classes on relief in this dominion. One class has been drawing relief since confederation. When a government does mot balance its budget, so that it must borrow more and more to meet deficits, it is certainly paying relief to the lenders in increasing volume. They are just as surely on relief as any other class, and we have been keeping them on relief ever since confederation. The other class are the recipients of direct relief in these days, the unemployed, and so on.
. I have a sentence about which I should like hon. members to think seriously. I say that the consumer should be the measuring stick . of all values. The day will come in this and every other country when the consumer will be the boss, because he has the franchise, and any government which neglects to look after the best interests of each and every consumer is not fulfilling its function as a government. The consumer, may I repeat, should be the measuring stick, and if we look to his welfare we are looking to the welfare of each and every one, and the prosperity of the country as a whole.
I ask myself: Why are the banks in such good financial condition, when most businesses are just tottering on the brink of bankruptcy and financial distress? There is a reason for that.

speechtext:
There were smiles on the faces of hon. members opposite when the hon. member for Lethbridge, when asked what he would do, said, "I would call in the bankers." I take it that when this government took office it did call in the bankers, and I believe it took their advice. I wonder if it called in the manufacturers, and asked them whether they would like more orders for their factories. I wonder whether it called in the retailers and asked them if they would like to sell more goods. I wonder if it called in labour, and asked them if they would like to go to work. I wonder if it called in the farmers and asked them if they would like a market for their produce. I wonder if it called in the unemployed and asked them what they thought of the situation. I wonder if it called in the housewives vrho, I see, are now organizing, and asked their opinions. Had the government got the advice of these parties, I think some different action would have been taken.
When the hon. member for Lethbridge was speaking, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) asked: "Can you give us any evidence of where anything of this nature has been tried and proved a success?" I should like to refer to New Zealand. Some hon. members may say, "Yes, but New Zealand has not a social credit government." I am informed that social credit candidates did not take part in the campaign of 1936 in New Zealand, but that in most constituencies the candidate was pledged to social credit principles. After the election it was discovered that on the government side there was a majority of social credit pledged members. So, while it is called a labour government, it is government pledged to social credit principles, and one which has worked along that particular line.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Are they giving $25 a month?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
The same criticism was made in New Zealand that has been made in this chamber. In 1935, prior to the election in that country, the same game was played. Here are some choice pieces of invective which were thrown at the labour party there: "Savings would be wiped out; insurance policies would be worthless; wages would be worthless." " If given power, the labour

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
party would wreck the banks and institutions to which you have entrusted your savings." " Their reckless experiment of creating credit would make all money worthless." " Why waste time talking about wages, pensions and spending power when wages would not be worth the paper they were printed on"? "Labour's talk about using public credit, to issue sufficient money to meet the needs of the nation, and the promise to mint and print it means only one thing-worthless money." " A hundred pounds would eventually be worth less than a hundred pence." " Savings, bank balances, and insurance policies would be wiped out."
But the people of New Zealand considered it was time to take a chance, and they got this result: Sixty-five thousand unemployed found work, and there are now $30,000,000 more in the savings banks than there were at the time these stupid words were spoken. Have not these same words been used in Canada? We are all familiar with the political mind which cannot rise above the traditions of the past, and which imagines the world would go to pieces if the people got a decent living.
The following is a newspaper article dealing with the situation in Australia:
Premier Savage, head of the first Labour government of New Zealand, had been tackled by the leader of the opposition on the subject of his declared intention to make use of the public credit. This term, his opponent, Adam Hamilton, professed to be unable to understand, which, by the way, is a failing that is also familiar to Canadians.
"My statements," replied Mr. Savage, "mean that we are going to use the public credit instead of going around by London or some other place. If we came in here to pursue the bad old ways, we would not be justifying the confidence the people placed in us at the last election. We are going to do the job the people asked us to do."
The method that had been adopted in the past, the premier said, had been to float loans on the London market. "We never got the money. Sometimes we got goods that we didn't particularly want. But we did get a huge national debt. To-day we are instituting a new method. We are going to use the public credit direct. We are going to carry our own obligations.
If the leader of the opposition cannot distinguish between a lending institution which the people own and one which is owned by somebody else I pity him. The difference is between pledging the public credit in order to produce upon it and pledging the public credit to raise debts upon it."
On the question of production Mr. Savage pointed out that New Zealand had had production before but it had seldom had prosperity. What good is production, he asked, if the benefit does not reach the producer?
"It is no use creating wealth unless the people have access to it. The money incomes of the people must equal the value of their production."
In the ten years preceding 1930 the farmers had doubled their production, yet their incomes remained the same. "But in the last twelve months during which the government has been guiding the industry, the national income has gone up by 20,000,000 pounds.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That sounds like social credit.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
That is in New Zealand, in the first year of operation. Then, we hav6 another statement from New Zealand, which is as follows:
The practicability of the New Zealand program is confirmed by the best of all tests and yardsticks-the immediate effect on consumer goods business volume, on which depend ultimately all capital goods activity, export trade, wage paying ability, dividend paying ability and tax paying ability.
In this connection it is interesting to note that in the newT government's first twelve months of office, their national production was up 18 per cent, industrial production 13J per cent, wages 13J per cent; building 24 per cent, savings deposits 15 per cent, and unemployment was down 32 per cent, to mention only a few of the evidences of steady improvement. Practically no woman is unemployed, and large numbers have left factories, shops and offices to get married.
The only way to cure our problem is to tackle it according to the best democratic plan available and then correct our mistakes, if any, as we proceed. The greatest mistake is to do nothing.
I should like to give in concrete form a few of the things which the government of New Zealand have done in one year of office. They nationalized their central bank one hundred per cent. Compare that with what Canada has done. The elections in Canada and New Zealand were held in the same year, 1935. Our present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) during the compaign promised the people of this country that if he were returned to power he would nationalize the central bank and restore to government the control of currency and credit, to be issued in terms of public need. He said that before the election. Premier Savage said it after he was elected, and that makes quite a difference.
Here are a few other things that were done by the New Zealand government within its first year of office. All classes of pensions were increased ; wages were restored to the 1931 level; a forty-hour working week was made universal with a few exceptions; wage scales are adjusted twice a year to the cost of living index; the price of dairy products is fixed by the government ; the 1937 program includes a comprehensive plan of health insurance and national superannuation.
The other achievements of the New Zealand government are maximum education possibilities for all children; balanced imports and

exports; the price of wheat, flour and bread has been stabilized; increased old age pensions, with women receiving the pension at sixty instead of sixty-five, and income, not property, is the deciding factor in determining the amount of pension paid; invalid pensions on a sliding scale; widows' pensions increased, and so on. I am sure that if any member wants to read a summary of the work of the first labour government, he will find it very interesting.
