maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although this debate has gone on for quite a few days, the only thing that seems to have been definitely settled so far is that every loan creates a deposit. However, I am doubtful of the efficacy of that conclusion to get us out of our difficulties. From my point of view I think it is about as useful a matter to discuss as which came first, the hen or the egg. At all events we have come to one conclusion.
I am glad that I am following the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Needham), particularly because of the subject with which he concluded his speech, as it is along that line I am going to speak to-night. I wish to show that a socialist government must inevitably follow a capitalist government if democracy is going to continue.
The government of New Zealand, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has pointed out, is not a social credit government. It is a labour or socialist government, carrying out within the limits of its power those things which socialists would do to rectify the faults of the present system.
When the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) moved his amendment, he

took occasion to deliver a lecture on social credit. I am not finding fault with my hon. friend for so doing. He and those sitting around him were sent here to give voice in this house to very definite ideas which they hold in regard to economic and social problems and the way in which they can be solved. He was only doing his duty in bringing that matter to the attention of the house in the way in which he did. Whether or not we agree with the theory of social credit, the debate has served a useful purpose. It has drawn to the attention of the house once again through the speeches of several members the tremendous inequality in the distribution of income in this country.
In the few words I am going to say to-night I am not going to take the position that there is no merit in the claims made by my hon. friends to my left. I suppose there is a modicum of truth and some error in all philosophies and in all social and economic creeds. I noticed, during the course of the speech of the hon. member for Lethbridge, that when he was asked specifically what his party would do, he invariably replied that they would call in the experts. That is a good answer under ordinary or even extraordinary circumstances, but in this case it is not satisfactory. It is not satisfactory because in the matter of the operation of social credit there are no experts to be called in.
If the hon. member for Lethbridge wanted to construct a road or a bridge or a house and wanted it well built, he would send for a man who had built roads or bridges or houses, depending upon what he wanted done. In other words, he would call in an experienced builder. He would not call in to build a house a man who had just written about building houses but had never built one. This, of course, is not to say that social credit is not feasible or easy of operation. But it does say that there are no social credit experts, because social credit is nothing but a theory. Major C. H. Douglas is not and could not be an expert in social credit, because there is no social credit system in operation anywhere where Major Douglas or anyone else could acquire the necessary experience to become an expert. No one knows that better than Major Douglas. That is why he keeps at a safe distance from the fields of actual operation.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: They might put him in gaol.

speechtext:
Not necessarily? That is what usually happens. Let me add that these debts can never be repaid, because they cannot be paid except with the property of those to whom we owe the debts.
I do not think we can have a clear understanding of the reason for the economic difficulties in which the world finds itself to-day unless we realize, as I have said, the real nature of capitalism; unless we realize that the purpose of capitalism is to produce more and more capital and not to provide for human wants. It does provide for human needs incidentally; but that is not its purpose, which is to create more and more capital. In order to explain the point I quote from a speech made a year or two ago by the Right Hon. Walter Elliot, former Minister of Agriculture in the British government; I think he is now Secretary for Scotland. Referring to the difficulties that the world was getting into at the time, he made this statement:
But these factors, the power of science to make anything anywhere, the determination of men to try everything everywhere, and a growing doubt as to whether foreign loans in many parts of the world are not simply free gifts which we should do as well to keep for ourselves, have produced and are producing a change so fundamental in our outlook that it
might almost be described as the third stage of the industrial revolution. The first stage was, so to speak, the drilling of a borehole and the tapping of a great subterranean source of power by the people who made this venture. The second, which we have just lived through, was the piping of that power to undeveloped nations as capital development, financed by unrepaid loans. The third stage is the check and flood-back as the bore holes in other countries strike oil in their turn, and the pipes begin to fill up from the far end also.
I do not see how the situation could be put much clearer than that. Let me explain briefly those stages. The first stage was the industrial revolution, beginning in England less than two hundred years ago, with the advent of motive power and machine production. The first result was to build up the capital structure of Great Britain: home industries. The second stage was the development of new countries, countries like North and South America, Australia and New Zealand. The third stage is where Mr. Elliot says that they have struck oil in the new countries and that there is a flood-back as the bore-holes fill up from the other end. So that in those countries into which, when capitalism was young, the older countries were putting their surplus investments, they now have surplus capital themselves and are look- [DOT] ing for a place to invest it. That is the world's condition at the present time, and it is a condition which the world is not going to get over under its present form of production and distribution.
I read what seemed to me a rather significant article in the January issue of Canadian Business, which I think is the official organ of the Canadian chamber of commerce. The author of this article is Courtland Elliott, described by the publishers as one of Canada's brilliant young economists. He says:
The periods of greatest prosperity in Canada have coincided with an inward flow of foreign capital. Such capital has been invested directly in Canadian enterprises or in securities, the proceeds of which have been used largely for construction or expansion. In either case the funds have resulted in the manufacture of capital goods and the employment of labour at good wages.
There are those who contend that Canada already has enough capital equipment for tho volume of business that is being done and for the size of the population we have to sustain. In the light of present conditions and shortterm realities that statement is probably true. Faced with restricted markets on the one hand and improved industrial technique on the other, it is evident that our existing capital equipment has not been unduly pressed in the recent period of recovery. Indeed the fact that new capital financing for industrial purposes in 1937 was lower than in many years, and Canada has not been a net borrower of outside capital for three years, might indicate

Use oj Canada's Financial Resources
either a lack of need or a lack of profitable employment for foreign and domestic capital in Canada.
If such a condition is permanent we would probably have to reconcile ourselves to a lower standard of living, a withering production organization, a rising tide of social dependency and financial instability.
I do not agree that it is necessary for us to do that. To me it seems amazing that at a time when the people of Canada along with the people of the rest of the world have in a way reached the position for which mankind has been striving all down through the ages, that is, economic security; when we have everything necessary to produce the things we need, we should say that because we cannot get markets; because we cannot use them for this and that, we must prepare for enduring misery and poverty. It is beyond my comprehension that intelligent people should agree to that. I claim it is not necessary, if we use the equipment for social ends; that is, building homes and in other ways improving the living conditions of our people.
Let me say that I am supporting the amendment. I am supporting it because in my opinion this government has not even tried to make the resources of the country and the machinery of production operate in the interests of the people.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE AND SUBAMENDMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
No; I am quite clear in my point of view. About five years ago the present Prime Minister, speaking in this house, outlined a comprehensive program of social reform, which he pledged that the Liberal party would put into effect if returned to office. I maintain that that pledge has not been kept. On that occasion he said, as reported at page 2508 of Hansard of 1933:
It has been said by some hon. members of the Progressive group that there should be a new motive in industry. May I say that I entirely agree with that.

That is the present Prime Minister speaking.
I believe that once the different groups in industry are represented in the control of industry we shall come to have a very different conception of industry generally. The conception that we have to-day is too largely that industry is primarily a source of revenue; the means whereby private gains may be reaped.
We had been pointing that out for years. At that time the Prime Minister accepted our point of view. But what has he done since he came into office to change the purpose of industry, or as he said himself, to give it a new purpose? I claim that he has done absolutely nothing.
In the same speech he went on to say, at page 2510:
The system of distribution of products needs overhauling. Distribution should be on a service at cost basis. The spread in price is too great, as any comparison of prices paid to producers with prices consumers have to pay will make self-evident.
Again I ask, What has the Liberal party done to reduce this spread? Again the answer is nothing. Then on the same page, 2510, he says:
Industry has been adversely affected by the control exercised over industry, not by industrial managers so much as by promoters and financiers. We believe the interlocking of directorates is one of the factors which, on the one hand, enables bankers to control industries-
I should like my hon. friends over here to listen to this:
-and on the other hand, enables industrialists to_ control the banks. It is our view that in this connection there is room for much in the way of reform.
There is still room for much in the way of reform, but I doubt very much that we shall see any reform in this direction on the part of this government. I think it was our view, before the Prime Minister took it as the view of the Liberal party. But what has this government done to break the control of the bankers and industrialists over the economic life of this country? Again the answer must be, Nothing. I quote now from the message given by the Prime Minister to the people of Canada on October 14, 1935, the evening of the last election day. Part of his message at that time was:
We take up at once as our supreme task the endeavour to end poverty in the midst of plenty, starvation and unnecessary suffering in a land of abundance, discontent and distress in a country more blessed by providence than any other on the face of the globe, and gain for individual lives, and for the nation as a whole that "health and peace, and sweet content" which is the rightful heritage of all.

Use oj Canada's Financial Resources
We still have poverty in the midst of plenty. We still have starvation and unnecessary suffering in a land of abundance. We still have discontent and distress in a country more blessed by providence than any other on the face of the globe, and we are still waiting for that "health and peace, and sweet content," which the Liberal party promised us on the day of their victory in 1935. What is more to the point, there is no indication that the government has any plan by which these desirable things mentioned by the Prime Minister may be brought about.
As a final word may I say that until some government takes definite and decisive action to bring our industries under social control and make them function for the welfare of the people instead of being used for their exploitation, as they are to-day, the difficulties we are now experiencing are going to remain with us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) is very general in its terms, and is something that one might expect at any time from an opposition member, especially in that corner of the house. But, as the hon. member explained in the course of his remarks, he confined his attack upon the government to the monetary system, and suggested that his so-called monetary system, social credit, would bring to this country prosperity and relieve us from debt, and that unemployment would fade away. Otherwise he was most complimentary. I should like to quote from his remarks as they appear in Hansard:
The government has tried everything but money reform. I am ready to say what I have said in a hundred places in this country, both on the platform and elsewhere, that as far as I can judge the government in power to-day has done everything it could possibly conceive of under the present system to improve the condition of our people. It is my judgment that the ministers are as energetic, as honourable and as earnest as men could possibly be. It is my belief that the members are ready to do their utmost. They disagree among themselves with regard to high and low tariffs and with regard to the advantages of trade with this and that country, but as far as they can see and come to agreement, they are doing the best they can. I do not hesitate one moment to say that.
Coming from a member of the opposition, this is a high tribute, and it does not seem to me that tributes of this kind come very frequently even from our own most ardent supporters. But we are told that the Liberal party is a marching force, always advancing, never arriving and never satisfied. So we
think that perhaps when the budget comes down and the three-way trade agreement is completed, we shall have made another step forward and shall have again advanced a little further with our ideas of better trade relations. Hon. members will note that the hon, gentleman, who is the leader of his group and who comes from the prairie provinces, thinks the government has made a pretty good job of its tariff so far.
On the other hand the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) feels that at present the Liberal party is injuring this country by lowering tariffs. This is the first we have heard of this complaint from the right hon. gentleman for some time. I can remember him only a year ago stating that the Liberal party had not lowered the tariff to any extent.
The right hon. gentleman spoke of duties and dumping duties, and as it is nearly eleven o'clock I wish to refer for a moment or two to one of those dumping duties. I am glad that dumping duties are passing from our customs rulings and that the customs authorities do not invoke them as they were invoked in the days of the previous administration. I believe dumping duties are dangerous, because they affect the whole fabric of our export trade. Canadian manufacturers should be against dumping duties except as a last resort, because a manufacturer who takes advantage of the drawbacks in duty and ships abroad, may be said to be dumping. So, when someone in a foreign country says that products are sent to that country at less than the cost in the country of origin, the manufacturer can hardly complain. At present in my part of Canada we hear a great deal about the dumping duty on sugar. That is something which affects my people. We feel that we should do a better trade with the republic of Cuba, whose tariff laws are very fair in that they say that if a country buys fifty per cent of its requirements from them, they will give that country the minimum tariff. In view of the fact that this is a potential market for our primary products, and because of the primaiy products Cuba can ship to us, I think the continuance of the dumping duty to the island of Cuba under present conditions is promoting an economic injustice.
The other day the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) told us what was in the speech from the throne in Nova Scotia, and he pointed out that in that province those on relief had been reduced from 75,000 to a little more than
6,000,	and that this was a record not equalled anywhere else in Canada. This is not because we have greater wealth in Nova Scotia;

Questions
the fact is that the per capita wealth in that province is only SI,514, as against a per capita wealth in Ontario of $2,468. It is due, rather, to the independence and individualism of our people. They do not like to submit to the indignities of being supported by the state. The municipal councils in our towns and municipalities guard against giving relief, where it is possible to avoid doing so, and they see to it that an honest day's work is given for the money spent on any of the projects carried on in the province.
On motion of Mr. Kinley the debate was adjourned.
